=== FILE: Lung Transplantation： How Late Referrals Impact Outcomes [MvRioYKnpg8].en.txt ===

Welcome to the podcast series from the specialists at Pen Medicine. I'm Melanie Cole and today we're discussing the waiting game, referral to lung transplantation, too little, too late, and how late referrals can impact outcomes. Joining me is Dr. Joshua Diamond. He's an associate medical director in the Penn Lung Transplant Program and an assistant professor of medicine at Penn Medicine. Dr. Diamond, it's a pleasure to have you join us today. Let's start with a little disease specific lung transplant considerations for key diagnosis. Give us some of those and why lung transplant would even be considered. There are several specific indications for lung transplantation in the United States and now worldwide. The number one indication is interstitial lung disease pulmonary fibrosis followed closely by COPD emphyma. The recommendation for referral for patients with interstitial lung disease really varies dependent on the type of lung disease that the patient has. The more likely the patient has a UIP or IPF diagnosis, the early their referral should be. The ultimate goal is getting patients in for initial meeting with a lung transplant team as early as possible during their course so that we can get to know the patient, learn what's going on, identify potential barriers to transplantation. For emphyma, on the other hand, transplantation is more of a quality of life improving procedure and not necessarily a length of life improving procedure. Therefore, the timing of referral is really dependent on a combination of both the severity of their disease and their quality of life. Patients with cystic fibrosis, which is the third most common indication for transplant, are really dependent on the severity of their exacerbations, the frequency of need for IV antibiotics, and other lung specific complications, hemoptsis, pulmonary hypertension. Patients with pulmonary hypertension as their primary indication, which would be the fourth most common indication, should really be referred when they have progressive disease requiring multiple different medications for control and start to have more signs of RV dysfunction and RV failure. Well, thank you for that. So, how does early referral for consideration impact survival? And what would you like to tell other providers about the importance of objectively assessing clinical decline? I think it's an important factor of getting patients in early. What we've noticed over the last five years or so is that patients are getting referred for transplant consideration later and later in their course because there are more and more options for treatment of many advanced lung diseases. The downside to this is that patients end up arriving in our offices, meeting us so late in their disease course that the amount of time that we have available to go through the evaluation phase, provide them education, provide their families education about what's involved in the transplant process isn't enough time. We've had patients who've gotten listed and then have had rapid decline after listing such that we've not had enough days, weeks, or months to be able to actually get them transplanted. So the goal of early referral is to maximize the likelihood that a patient will end up being a candidate, be well educated in what's required to make a good candidate both for them and their families, and then provide sufficient time for a suitable match to be identified such that they can be transplanted successfully. Our goal is to transplant patients when they're within a window in which they're still healthy enough to get the maximum benefit from transplantation because there is an entity of being too sick for transplant. Although that has really shifted further and further away as our ability to maintain and transplant sick patients has improved. So I'd like you to speak about patient selection. Dr. Diamond, is this based on specific protocol-driven multiddisciplinary assessment? What does the transplant evaluation process look like at Pen Medicine? The process kind of depends on how sick the patient is at the time that we meet them first. We have three different pathways that patients can go through. If patients are on the healthier side, often times they'll come meet one of our pulmonologists for an initial assessment. It's typically an hour-ong visit. We'll review their history, review their records, and provide them significant education about the transplant process and then make a decision about whether the patient is appropriate to move forwards with evaluation or whether more monitoring or evaluation is required. If patients are a bit sicker but still as an outpatient, often times we will have a concurrent first visit along with our evaluation and our evaluation is 4 days of outpatient testing. It's extremely extensive. We do multiple referrals to our consultants. They include a nurse, respiratory therapist, physical therapist, speech pathologist, social worker, cardiac surgeon, financial person. I'm sure I'm leaving out somebody else. There's about nine different people that they meet with. They also meet with our research team. And then we get CT scans, blood tests, ultrasounds, heart testing, vascular testing. And it's organized over a 4-day period. About a week later, we meet as a large multi-disiplinary team, discuss the entire case, and then come up with a plan going forwards as to what is needed. Now, if patients are even sicker and are already inatients or require inpatient care, we actually will transfer patients to the hospital and do that evaluation entirely as an inpatient. And we we've done evaluations on people who are ambulatory all the way through full mechanical ventilation, ECMO support, regardless of how sick they are. Those patients typically have a very short window of potential transplantation and so we try to get that evaluation done as quickly as possible but the input for the decision making regarding listing is made by all of the people who are involved in that evaluation process for other providers. Dr. Diamond, what are the absolute contraindications to lung transplant? This has really changed over the last 10 to 15 years and the number of absolute contraindications is kind of a moving target. What we've tried to get our referring physicians to do is to send us a message, give us a phone call so that we can discuss patients because often times things that start out as absolute contraindications can be intervened upon or fixed. For example, one of the strict criteria that we use is BMI. And we require patients to have a BMI less than 35. But we have had patients who have been referred with significantly higher BMIs. And we've provided them education or nutritional support in how to appropriately lose weight such that they become appropriate candidates. Other things to consider are things like profound frailty. And so we have a large program at Penn engaged in trying to mitigate frailty in the pre-transplant phase of care. There are other types of infections that are specifically considered to be likely to be absolute contraindications. Things like mcoacterium obsessis active infection and burlarius sepatia infection in patients with cystic fibrosis. But in general, our goal as a team is to try to maximize the likelihood that somebody will be able to become a candidate and oftentimes we're able to intervene upon fix or mitigate things that had historically been considered absolute contraindications. So interesting. Thank you for that answer. Can you highlight for us any progress on the weight list management of disease, possibly reducing those waiting times? What can a patient expect once they've been placed on the transplant list? And tell us about this experience. How waiting time is calculated? What are you doing now? Wait time varies from person to person. And it's common for patients to ask, "How long do you think I'm going to wait for transplantation, but there are several factors that go into how long somebody's going to wait. The first is how sick the patient is." In essence, the scoring system that's used for lung allocation is the lung allocation score. The LA tries to estimate the likelihood of survival with and without a transplant. And it tries to maximize the difference. In that case, the sicker you are, the higher the score is going to be. And so for patients who are significantly sick, we have them come in for frequent reassessments because the numbers that are utilized to calculate that score can change from a momentto- moment basis. They can have progressively worsening lung function. They can have increasing oxygen requirements. And so the expectation for weight time is directly tied to the severity of illness. At the same time, there are other factors that come into play. The lungs need to fit in the thoracic cavity. So taller people need bigger lungs, shorter people need smaller lungs. Other factors that go into the decision or the amount of time, blood type, as well as other factors related to immune compatibility, specifically related to human lucasite antigen or HLA compatibility. And this is related to whether somebody has had a prior pregnancy, prior blood transfusion, autoimmune disease, or prior organ transplantation. And all of those factors come into play when trying to estimate how long somebody's going to wait. I typically quote people that the average survival is about 3 months, but at the level of the individual, that average might not be applicable. We've had patients who have been listed and transplanted within days and we have patients who have unfortunately had to wait one to two years in order to get transplanted. So that leads well into the next question. As we're getting ready to wrap up, Dr. Diamond, tell us about the future of lung transplantation. What are some of the constraints to meeting the annual demand for lung transplantation and some of the issues and challenges that you see? So one of the issues is that there are more people who need lungs and other solid organs than our organs available. And so one of the goals is trying to maximize the donor pool. So here at Penn recently we completed a study evaluating the safety and utility of utilizing donors who have hepatitis C viral infection and demonstrated that we can safely treat hepatitis C after organ transplantation. accepting organs from donors who have hepatitis C can significantly increase the donor pool. There are other factors that were interested in trying to improve organ function. Things like predictive algorithms for how a lung is going to function after transplantation. better understanding of the impact of the different donor risk factors, things like donor smoking, donor drug use, donor age, and how they play into outcomes after lung transplantation. There's a lot of efforts on our research side of trying to both maximize the utility of donors and then maximize the likelihood that a recipient is going to survive. We have a very large research enterprise focused on the perry transplant period of care and how to maximize the likelihood that somebody's going to get the full benefit from organ transplantation. Dr. Diamond, as we wrap up, kind of summarize the recommendations for timing of referral, the benefits of earlier referral, and if there's an issue if a provider refers a patient too early. I think the ultimate goal of most transplant programs and ours in particular is to have patients referred to early. We are happy to follow along with the primary pulmonologist in the community and help to gauge the proper time for actual formal evaluation and potential listing. But the sooner we get to know the patient, the more comfortable the patient will feel with us as their potential providers and the more comfortable we will feel with being able to move forwards with the transplant process. There's really no downside to early referral because of the fact that you get open access to the program and all of the resources that are available to the patient at the level of social work and nutrition and other potential consultations. We help to guide the timing of when testing should be happening such that we can minimize the likelihood that patients are going to need to have repetitive in-person or invasive testing. We as a team are really open to having discussions with community and referring physicians about patients at the individual level. We're happy to have phone calls. Our expanded use of Zoom and other remote technology has really enabled us to be more open and available to have those types of discussions. We would prefer too early or early rather than too late from a referral perspective because we've had patients who have unfortunately not been able to benefit from transplant because of referral too late. === FILE: MS & Pregnancy [kMXjj0Azom0].en.txt ===

While pregnancy is safe to undertake, there are specific risks for women with MS trying to conceive. Welcome to the podcast series from the specialists at Pen Medicine. I'm Melanie Cole and joining me today is Dr. Rachel Brandsteader. She's an assistant professor of clinical neurology at Penn Medicine and she's part of the Penn Multiple Sclerosis Center. We're discussing MS and pregnancy today and Dr. Branded, thank you so much. You've been on with us before, so welcome back. When we last spoke, you explained that MS is more likely to impact women between the ages of 20 and 40 years old, and you noted the importance of discussing family planning with patients. You mentioned that while pregnancy is safe to undertake, there are specific risks for women with MS when they're trying to conceive. Can you please speak about those concerns and how they can be addressed for women with MS that are planning a family? Certainly, and thank you for having me back. Firstly, for patients interested in pursuing pregnancy, it's important to note that multiple sclerosis itself does not seem to increase the risk for infertility, adverse pregnancy outcomes, or adverse neonatal outcomes. For many years, the effect of pregnancy on MS disease was somewhat uncertain. However, this did change with the landmark pregnancy NMS or PRIM study that was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in the late 1990s, which examined 256 pregnancies and demonstrated a decreased risk for MS relapse during pregnancy, particularly in the third trimester. This finding has since been corroborated in more modern investigations and has been encouraging for patients and providers alike. The PRIM study also heralded work that revealed an increased risk for relapse in the first 3 to four months postpartum, particularly for women with active disease prior to pregnancy, which includes clinical symptoms or MRI activity. This highlights the importance of achieving good control of MS in advance of pregnancy and the need to discuss family planning with patients as early as possible, even around the time of diagnosis. So if a patient with MS is beginning to think about starting her family, what would be your recommended next steps and tell us about the services that Penn Medicine offers along the way? So if a patient with MS is considering starting a family, I would recommend that they discuss this as early as possible with their MS neurologist to ensure that there has not been any recent MS disease activity, again clinical or MRI. And for those on disease modifying treatments for their multiple sclerosis, it's important to discuss the safety of either continuing these medications through conception or the appropriate interval for discontinuation or wash out from the drug in advance of conception. The PENMS center has providers and pharmacists who are experts in preconception and intrapartum counseling and can help provide an individualized approach for a patient and their family throughout this process. So doctor, relapse is always a concern for any individual with MS. Are there therapies that can help mitigate that risk of relapse before or during conception and pregnancy? As I mentioned earlier, good control of MS disease in advance of pregnancy is very important for mitigating the risk for relapse both during conception and during pregnancy. There are MS disease modifying therapies which can provide a more durable or long-lasting protection against relapse without fetal exposure to the medication. One example is okralismab which is a B cell targeting amunotherapy delivered via an intravenous infusion every 6 months. It is one of several highly effective disease modifying therapies in our treatment toolkit for preventing relapses and new MRI lesions. This medication could be administered and patients can wait an appropriate interval before attempting conception. My practice is around 2 to 3 months after infusions and have some security that they are both protecting themselves from MS disease activity but not exposing their baby to the medication. There are several other strategies for lowering the risk for relapse during pregnancy including continuation of some MS disease modifying therapies even during conception and pregnancy. And what about the postpartum period and if women are breastfeeding, where do those medications fit into this picture? So in the postpartum period, we aim to prevent inflammatory activity and that's going to involve individualized decisions regarding the patients breastfeeding plans, when to resume disease modifying therapy, and how to select the appropriate treatment. I often recommend a surveillance MRI of the brain at around four to six weeks postpartum to monitor for subclinical disease activity. If a woman elects not to breastfeed, we may aim to resume treatment as early as two to four weeks postpartum. There are data, however, that suggests that exclusive breastfeeding extends the protective period against relapse. And thus, if a patient does elect to breastfeed, there are options to either remain off of disease modifying therapy while nursing, particularly if that postpartum MRI is stable without new lesions, or for those patients with high risk for postpartum relapse, there is an option to breastfeed while on certain disease modifying therapies. More data is needed in our field to confirm the safety of this strategy. It's also important for MS providers to comprehensively evaluate the patients functioning postpartum. Evaluating her mood, physical function, sphincter issues, and to utilize a multidisciplinary approach to care as needed. Well, that leads me well into my next question. And how do you advise patients and their providers, whether it's their gynecologist, and obstitrician or their MS neurologist about managing physical health side effects and mental health? because it can be pretty scary to be pregnant with MS. Well, I certainly encourage close care with both the MS neurologist and the obstitricians as part of the team and to manage all of these symptoms as they come up and to remain attentive to them also in the postpartum period. There's not any specific strategy for instance treating postpartum depression in patients with MS compared with patients who don't have MS. But just to remember that a woman with MS is still a woman going through all of the other challenges of pregnancy and to stay as attentive to those as possible. And for instance, one specific example would be if a patient with MS already has some impacts of MS on the bladder to think about the way urinary symptoms might be exacerbated in the postpartum period after delivery and be more likely to consider strategies such as pelvic floor rehabilitation for such a patient. That's very good advice. What about long-term impacts of pregnancy on the MS disease course? What do we know about that now? So despite the potential for increased relapse risk postpartum, the majority of individuals do not experience relapses in the postpartum period and pregnancy does not appear to alter long-term relapse rate or the risk for disease progression. However, the impact of pregnancy on long-term MS outcomes does remain less clear and there are some mixed data. So we have more to learn about this for sure. Dr. brand stutter. As we get ready to wrap up, is there anything else you'd like referring providers to know of before they refer a patient to the MS and Women's Health Center and the specialists at Penn Medicine? What would you like the lasting message to be about MS and pregnancy? I encourage all providers to start preconception counseling for MS patients early on, even at diagnosis. Providers should feel empowered to refer to our women's health division within our MS center for support in this counseling at any stage of family planning, but particularly early on when the decision regarding disease modifying therapies are being made. I also would empower those providers to give an optimistic message to their patients with MS that they can pursue family planning safely and that there are a lot of strategies in place to help them have happy and healthy pregnancies. Thank you so much Dr. Bransteader for joining us today to refer your patient to Dr. Bransteader at Penn Medicine. Please call our 247 provider only line at 8779377366 or you can submit your referral via our secure online referral form by visiting our website at penmed.org/refer your patient. That concludes this episode from the specialists at Pen Medicine for updates on the latest medical advancements. breakthroughs and research. Please follow us on your social channels. I'm Melanie Cole.

Welcome to the podcast series from the specialists of Pen Medicine. I'm Melanie Cole and I invite you to listen as we discuss MS and women's health at Penn Medicine. There are genomewide association studies that have implicated over 200 independent genetic lossi for multiple sclerosis. One single nucleotide polymorphism on the X chromosome has been associated with multiple sclerosis. There have not been any such susceptibility alals found on the Y chromosome. We don't fully understand the scope of that gene's function, but it is interesting that it's seen on the X chromosome rather than the Y chromosome and may explain a little bit about why multiple sclerosis is more common in women. There is also very likely an interaction between the genome and sex specific biological and environmental factors that may underly the possible increase in MS incidents seen in women. Sex hormones very clearly play a role in the development of MS as we see that puberty represents a risk factor for MS as does earlier age of menarchy. Though these biological mechanisms have to be more fully fleshed out. There's also a strong link between pregnancy and MS as one study found that having children reduced the risk of MS in women but not in men by about 46% in the following 5 years. It's possible that low levels of estrogen that are associated with menstruation have a more stimulating effect on the immune system while higher estrogen levels like those seen during pregnancy might exhibit a more immunosuppressive effect. And as I mentioned, there are several environmental factors that have been identified as increasing the risk for multiple sclerosis, including smoking, Epstein bar virus, seropositivity, low serum vitamin D levels, and low sunlight exposure. So these factors may also interact with biological sex to increase the risk for multiple sclerosis in women. Wow, that's so interesting. So, do MS symptoms onset occur in predictable patterns in women? Doctor, are there times of life when they're more likely to experience these symptoms or that the symptoms are exacerbated? Yes, MS is more likely to impact women between the ages of 20 and 40 years old. This highlights the importance actually of discussing family planning with our patients, including pregnancy and breastfeeding. There have been several studies also that have attempted to determine if menopause affects MS disease course. Some of these studies have noted a worsened disability acrual around menopause, but others have not borne that out. So then speak a little bit about the commonality in both sexes. You've already spoken about how they're worse in women. Are there any common symptoms, things that you've noticed that you'd like other providers to know where you could link the two sexes? So multiple sclerosis presents with a very common set of symptoms that we see equally in men and women. Those are impairments in visual functioning, symptoms related to spinal cord dysfunction like weakness, numbness or tingling, spasticity or muscle tightness, gate dysfunction. We also see other symptoms such as brain stem symptoms such as double vision or vertigo and cognitive dysfunction in all of our patients with MS. But again, many of the symptoms of MS are common to men and women, but they might be experienced a bit differently. For example, neurologic bladder dysfunction from MS may be heightened by bladder dysfunction related to pelvic floor weakness from prior childirth in women. So now let's talk about treatments that are specifically available for women with MS. We have so many medications now to help treat multiple sclerosis. Most of these are common to men and women. But there are a few interesting research interests for women specifically. So research conducted in animal models of multiple sclerosis suggested a protective effect of high doses of estrogen. Two randomized phase 2 clinical trials evaluated the impact of exogenous hormones on MS disease course. In these studies, an oral estrogen called ethanol estradiol was added to standard injectable disease modifying MS therapies and patients were treated both with the traditional MS therapy and estrogen. And those that got both treatments demonstrated fewer inflammatory lesions on brain MRI and a lower rate of clinical relapses than those who were treated with the MS therapy alone. There was encouragingly a suggestion of a positive impact on cognitive disability in these studies as well. This is being further investigated with dedicated clinical trials. Here at Penn Medicine, we are part of these phase three clinical trial efforts to better study the effect of exogenous hormones to help our women with MS. So tell us a little bit about what makes your program stand apart. What's unique about the program at Penn Medicine? Tell us a little bit about the multidisciplinary team and what that means for these patients. Here at Pen Medicine, we are a dynamic multiddisciplinary team that are here first and foremost to help patients with multiple sclerosis and related disorders. We follow this comprehensive care model in order to address all of our patients needs. So, we have attending neurologists. We have three expert nurse practitioners who help us take care of patients. We have nurses who coordinate care and care for our patients. We have a social worker who is dedicated, knowledgeable, and empathic and there to help our patients with the many ways that MS affects their personal and professional lives. And we have clinical pharmacists who are experts on all of our MS disease modifying and symptomatic medications that are there just to educate, counsel, and support our patients and help them navigate their drug treatment for MS. Do you have any final thoughts you'd like to leave other providers with when you feel it's important they refer to the specialists at Penn Medicine and what you'd like them to know about women's health and MS? The field of multiple sclerosis care has become ever more complex and there are so many treatments both disease modifying and symptomatic that we offer our patients here at Penn Medicine. So a consultation with us is a great idea when somebody is newly diagnosed to confirm diagnosis when someone's about to initiate a treatment or even when somebody's facing some symptoms that might be challenging. We are here to provide that additional layer of support and use all of the resources that I mentioned earlier to help improve the lives of our patients with MS. There are many opportunities for a referral to our team at pen medicine for a patient where we need to confirm the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, initiate a treatment or for patients who are having difficulty with symptom management. Importantly, a good time to refer your patient for a consultation with us at Pen Medicine would be to discuss complex issues around family planning and pregnancy and to help women with MS deal with symptoms during the menopausal period. === FILE: Measuring Health in Our Communities ｜ Penn Medicine’s Data-Driven Approach to Health Equity [ChIHuu34XNk].en.txt ===

At Penn Medicine, we're committed to uplifting the communities we serve. To truly improve health outcomes, we need to understand our communities on a deeper level. Philadelphia faces significant challenges. As one of the poorest big cities in the US, nearly 20% of residents live in poverty. What's striking is how geography impacts health. Life expectancy can vary by up to 15 years from one zip code to another. But it's also a city with tremendous vitality and connected communities. We want to build on that strength while helping to address the challenges our communities face. To address these disparities, we developed a comprehensive approach to measure health in our communities. We focused on five key indicators. Poverty rates, food insecurity rates, hypertension diagnosis and control, colurectal and breast cancer screening, and immunization rates for respiratory infections. We measured each indicator at the zip code level for Penn Medicine's downtown Philadelphia catchment area, comparing results to city, state, and national rates. The findings revealed significant opportunities. High poverty and food insecurity alongside gaps in preventive care. Most importantly, communities with higher poverty consistently had worse outcomes across multiple health metrics. But we're not just identifying problems, we're implementing solutions. Pen Medicine has been running a remote hypertension management program for nearly a decade with proven results. I work at Pen Medicine and live in North Philadelphia. The program gave me a blood pressure cuff and sends text messages to check my readings. A nurse and a doctor review my results and help me find the right medications to control my blood pressure. We've also invested in a mobile mimography unit to increase screening access for our most vulnerable patients. This work is about understanding our community's needs so we can respond with precision and care. By identifying where disparities exist, we can focus our resources where they'll have the greatest impact. At Penn Medicine, we believe all patients deserve a long, healthy life, regardless of their zip code. We're using these insights to reduce disparities and build healthier communities across Philadelphia.

=== FILE: Measuring the Impact of Liquid Biopsy on Clinical Decision Making for NSCLC Patients [d8Cn1hynTIg].en.txt ===

a liquid biopsy is a way in which we can use a very simple blood test a single tube of a patient's blood to obtain information about the tumor we do this by isolating from that tube of blood cells and DNA that have been shed by the tumor and then we use that to identify genetic information that's actually driving the growth of the tumor imagine an advanced lung cancer patient who has a tumor not only in the lungs but also in the bone in the brain we're able to detect each of those mutations and we can stop the growth of the tumor and in fact we showed in a recent study that for 102 lung cancer patients half of them had surgically inaccessible tumor locations meaning that a liquid biopsy was the only way to guide the Precision of their care so the reason we're doing this study is to use for the first time hard evidence on a large number of patients to measure and quantify the benefit in survival to our patients when we use Liquid biopsy and this is precision medicine at pen

I realized quickly in medical school that you're able to fix the heart and get immediate feedback, so you can leave the operating room and know that you fixed a patient's problem. The focus of my work is on coronary revascularization and advanced techniques in coronary revascularization. The field has developed a lot since the 1960s when the first coronary bypass procedure was done, and that's taking veins or arteries from a part of the body and bypassing obstructions in the heart that cause coronary disease, or angina, or chest pain. What I am able to do is to do advanced techniques where we can do these procedures off the bypass machine, where we don't need to arrest the heart, where we can keep the heart beating while we do the procedure, which lowers complications for the patient, And also using arteries throughout the body, using the arteries in the chest, using the radial artery. These arteries have better patency long-term than if we were just to use veins. One of the other areas of interest is the minimally invasive approaches in coronary artery surgery, which involves using the robot to take down the internal thoracic mammary artery in the chest wall, and then through a small incision on the left side we can complete this procedure without opening the chest. This results in smaller incisions, less pain, quicker recovery, and getting out of the hospital with less complications. When we're deciding on whether or not a patient needs surgery, it's a patient-centered decision and it's shared decision-making. We'll give them their options, and those options will include surgery, stenting, or medical therapy. We'll provide data for each of those options, and then based upon what they would prefer, we can then make a surgical plan, or a medical therapy plan, or a plan where the patient can get stented by their cardiologist. I think the most exciting thing is to take people who are having issues, having chest pain, having shortness of breath with exertion and not living the life that they want, and then seeing them and helping them form a plan where we can fix that.

thick that's about the size of a sharp pencil Point stage 2 melanomas are more than 2 mm thick stage stream means the tumor has spread to the local lymph nodes lymph nodes are small bean-shaped collections of immune system tissue throughout the body local means the lymph nodes are near the tumor so if a melanoma is on the forearm and it spread to the lymph nodes in the armpit it would be stage three melanoma stage four means that the melanoma has spread to distant areas of the body such as the lungs liver or brain hello I'm Dr Christopher Miller to determine the stage of a melanoma the healthcare team conducts a patient evaluation this process involves a biopsy and a thorough medical history and physical exam some patients but not all also have medical tests to see if the melanoma has spread to other parts of the body in a biopsy a small sample of the skin tissue with melanoma is removed and studied under a microscope the biopsy helps confirm the type of melanoma the four types of melanoma are superficial spreading melanoma which is the most common type Leno maligna melanoma which tends to occur in older people and usually begins in areas that have had a lot of sun exposure nodular melanoma which often appears rapidly as a bump on the skin and acrolentiginous melanoma which develops on Palms soles or under the nail bed and is not related to sun exposure the biopsy also assesses certain features in the melanoma that can predict whether it has spread from the skin to inside the body the spreading of cancer is called metastasis the most important feature to predict whether the melanoma may have metastasized is the tumor's thickness thicker melanomas have a higher risk of metastasis other factors predicting a higher risk include a microscopic ulcer on the surface of the melanoma and the presence of mitosis which are microscopic signs that the melanoma cells are dividing rapidly the next step in the evaluation process is a thorough history and physical from the doctor during an office visit the doctor takes the patients medical and family histories and performs a complete physical examination which includes a total skin and lymph node examination based on the features of the melanoma under the microscope and any findings on the history or physical exam additional medical or surgical tests may be used to see if melanoma has spread in metastasis melanoma cells can reach other parts of the body by traveling through the lymph vessels and bloodstream although any organ can be affected by metastasis the most common internal organs affected by melanoma metastasis are the lungs and liver for this reason the following tests are often done a chest x-ray to evaluate the lungs liver blood tests and another blood test called the LDH test note that not everyone has these tests done if the biopsy indicated a low risk for metastasis the doctor may not recommend these tests for patients at higher risk for metastasis doctors sometimes recommend additional Imaging studies such as CT scans of the chest abdomen and pelvis to search for metastasis patients at higher risk include those whose primary melanoma is thicker than 4 mm and those whose melanoma has spread to lymph nodes however when first diagnosed with melanoma the majority of patients do not need these additional Imaging tests for most melanomas the first step in treatment is complete surgical removal of the primary tumor the primary tumor is the place on your skin where the melanoma was first detected this surgical removal is different from the initial biopsy where the main purpose was simply to remove enough skin cells to study them under the microscope the surgical removal of the tumor is often referred to as a wide excision because it's necessary to remove an area of normal tissue surrounding the melanoma to make sure that no melanoma cells are left behind the goal of the wide excision is to remove the cancer before it has a chance to spread inside the body the amount of tissue removed depends primarily on how thick the tumor is for example if your tumor is less than 1 mm deep the surgeon usually takes a margin of 1 cm of normal tissue if the tumor is 2 mm thick or more your surgeon May recommend removing 2 cenm of normal tissue around the melanoma this amount of normal tissue is much smaller than what was commonly removed in the past Studies have shown that large surgical excisions are no longer required the surgeon's goal is to ensure that the melanoma is removed completely when the melanoma is dark brown or black in a background of lighter colored skin the naked eye is very good at seeing the edges of the melanoma however if there are many pigmented spots around the site of of the melanoma or if the melanoma does not have a dark color it may be difficult for the surgeon to determine where the melanoma starts and stops using the naked eye alone in these instances the doctor May recommend Mo micrographic surgery to make sure that the melanoma is completely removed Mo surgery is a highly specialized technique in which the surgeon removes the visible portions of the melanoma and immediately examines 100% of the edges under the microscope if the mo surgeon detects microscopic areas of cancer that were not visible to the naked eye he or she will remove more of the skin where the cancer Still Remains this process of removing areas of skin affected by melanoma and examining them under the microscope continues until the cancer is completely removed note that Mo surgery is a highly specialized technique and should be performed by a mo surgeon experienced in the treat treatment of melanoma another surgical procedure appropriate for some patients who are newly diagnosed with melanoma is Sentinel lymph node mapping and it can determine whether melanoma has spread to the lymph nodes The Sentinel node is the lymph node to which a cancer is likeliest to spread first in the mapping procedure the surgeon makes a small incision and removes the Sentinal node then the node is examined under a microscope if no melanoma is found in the Sentinel lymph node then no further lymph node surgery is needed if melanoma is detected in the Sentinel node surgery to remove the remaining lymph nodes in the area is usually recommended removing lymph nodes with microscopic areas of melanoma may help to slow the growth of melanoma Sentinel lymph node mapping is the best current test to determine whether melanoma has spread inside the body it is usually usually recommended for patients whose primary melanoma === FILE: Men's Health： Fact or Fiction [zG1sLnnBrCw].en.txt ===

To all the men out there, listen up. If you think you know the truth about the things that affect your body, think again. I’m Dr. Jeff Tokazewski from Penn Medicine, and I’m here to clear up what’s fact and what’s fiction when it comes to men’s health. Myth #1: Wearing a hat or using a blow-dryer will make you go bald. Take it from me, this one is FICTION! There is no scientific evidence that backs this claim. The average man can lose as much as 80 to 100 strands of hair daily, but your hat is only catching these hairs, not causing your hair loss. Baldness is mostly genetic, but can also be caused or worsened by stress, overusing hair products filled with chemicals, or hormonal imbalances. So, unless your hat is so tight that it’s cutting the circulation to your hair follicles, feel free to keep that cap on. Myth #2: Men who wear briefs have fewer sperm. This one is FICTION! Some argue that tight briefs hold the scrotum too close to the body, which warms the testicles and creates a harmful environment for sperm. While it’s true that extreme heat isn’t good for fertility, this level of warmth generally won’t put your semen at risk. Rather than changing your underwear, you’re better off avoiding hot tubs and keeping your lap top off your lap. Myth #3: Men hit their sexual peak at 18. Sorry gentlemen, but this one is a FACT! A man’s production of testosterone does in fact peak at around 18 years old. This means that the speed and firmness of your erections will be at their best at this age. But there’s no reason to panic just yet! While testosterone levels do decline as we get older, the decline doesn’t necessarily result in decreased stamina or sexual desire. So fellas, when it comes to your health, take a deep breath and consider that maybe some of these old wives’ tales can be left in the past. If you have questions about your health, talk to your primary care doctor. To learn more about Penn Primary Care, visit our website and stay healthy out there!

=== FILE: Migraines： Fact vs Fiction with Dr. Jeffrey Millstein [repQ_eRRCpg].en.txt ===

If you're one of the 37 million Americans who suffer from migraines, you know how frustrating it can be to get one, and even more so, to hear the misconceptions that people have about them. I'm Dr. Jeff Millstein with Penn Medicine, and today, we're going to find out what's fact and what's fiction when it comes to migraines. Migraines can bring on a number of symptoms including difficulty speaking, constipation or diarrhea, fatigue, dizziness or vertigo, and the one that leads us to our first myth - headaches. Myth 1: A migraine is just a bad headache. Though many people believe it, this one is FICTION! A bad headache is just one of many possible symptoms of a migraine attack. Migraine attacks can actually occur with no headache at all, which is known as a "silent" migraine. Migraines exist in four possible phases and the headache comes in phase 3. However, it IS possible to have a migraine without ever getting a headache. In fact, in order for a doctor to diagnose a migraine, you must have symptoms outside of just a headache. Myth 2: Migraines can last for multiple days. Unfortunately, this one is a FACT. In children, migraines typically last about an hour, but for adults, it could be anywhere from a few hours to more than three days. If you suffer from migraines, your primary care doctor may be able to prescribe medication to ease your pain. If your symptoms persist for longer than 72 hours, you should seek immediate medical attention. Myth 3: Migraines are caused by psychological factors like stress, anxiety and depression. It's widely believed, but this one is FICTION! While the cause of migraines isn't fully understood, we do know that migraines are a neurological condition, not a psychological one. Migraines are caused by a dysfunction in the nervous system that causes your brain's blood vessels to narrow, then expand, creating a pulsing pain that many people associate with a headache. Studies have also found that migraines tend to run in families, pointing to a hereditary factor with this condition. Stress can certainly play a role in triggering a migraine, but it is not the cause. Some known triggers include things like overexposure to certain noises, smells, or light, weather patterns, and changes in your sleep schedule. If you suffer from migraines, you can talk to your primary care provider about ways to manage your symptoms. To learn more about Penn Primary Care, visit our website... and stay healthy out there!

=== FILE: Minimally Invasive Foot & Ankle Surgery ｜ Penn Orthopaedics [BLR9V1opl6I].en.txt ===

There's a new technique that's revolutionizing foot and ankle reconstructive surgery. Today, I'm going to show you how we're using it to help our patients here at Penn Medicine. Hi, I'm Dr. Bobby Ndu, an orthopaedic surgeon at Penn Medicine, and I want to share with you some of the new and exciting advancements in minimally invasive foot and ankle surgery. These techniques have allowed us to take procedures that used to require large formal incisions and their subsequent dissections down to being done using incisions the size of a keyhole. Using a smaller incision means that there is significantly less soft tissue dissection, which means less scarring, less pain and swelling, and often a faster recovery with an easier return to activity for our patients. But, like any kind of surgery, minimally invasive surgical techniques still carry risks, such as bleeding, infection, or damage to adjacent anatomy, to name a few. Let's start by looking at one of the procedures you may have heard about: A minimally invasive bunion correction. So we first begin by making a small incision on the side of the toe, and that's about the extent of the incision that we need to start our procedure. After we make this incision that's about the size of the blade, we then take our cutting instrument, which is a low-speed, high-torque burr, and verify our position on x-ray. We're very particular about the angle at which we make that cut, to make sure we get the most optimum correction. We use the burr to make our cut through the bone, which allows us to start the process now of correcting the bunion. We then proceed to shift the bone over into its new position, and that is highlighted here by our instrument that is passed down the canal of the first metatarsal, and represents a block to the metatarsal head, pushing it laterally, creating our correction. After we have verified that we're happy with our shift and position, we place two K-wires into position through a separate keyhole incision to help hold the head in its new place. And then we verify on our x-ray that we're happy with the position of the bone and the wires before we commit to anything. After we place the initial guidewire, we place a second one parallel to it just to give us additional fixation, and to ensure that what we're trying to create is a stable construct. We then measure to determine the length of screw that we will need to pass over the wires to leave in as our permanent implant. We proceed to overdrill the wires to make room for the screws, and this is all being done through the second keyhole incision. We can appreciate our instrument still holding our metatarsal head shifted, and our temporary fixation of our guidewires coming here from the base of the metatarsal. Once we’ve verified that we've drilled to the appropriate depth, we then place our screws over the wires to give us our permanent fixation. And now, we can see that we have placed our screws over the guidewire, and you can appreciate that the head of this screw is quite specially shaped to match the metatarsal shaft and ensure it will not cause any soft tissue irritation, given the trajectory that is required for us to connect the metatarsal shaft to the head in its newly realigned position. And we can see here the relatively small nature of the two incisions that we've had to use now to accomplish this: one that can be visualized right here where our screws entered, and the second incision up here, where we made the original cut to the bone that allowed us to correct the bunion. Now, if we were to do this as a classic open Chevron osteotomy, the incision would have to be much broader, requiring significantly greater dissection to allow us exposure of the bone to make the appropriate cuts. We need to come through the skin, the underlying muscle, as well as the capsule that surrounds the joint, to give us access to the bone before we can even begin to make our cuts. And here you can see me moving the tissues aside still, before we would have even started the procedure. One of the beautiful things about minimally invasive surgery is we have avoided all of this, and we've been able to do the same procedure through a keyhole incision that is significantly smaller than what you see in front of you here now. So now, let's look at the difference of that open incision versus what we did earlier with the minimally invasive. You can see here the increased risk, time, and effort that's required for an open approach as opposed to the simple elegance of the small incision of an MIS approach. And that is why we're moving the majority of our patients to a minimally invasive approach, because of what it means for them and their recovery. Let's take a look at a minimally invasive hammer toe correction. Now, you can see that we have already made our keyhole incision, and now we're passing our instrument in, because we're already down to bone and our dissection is complete. We enter the bone with a low-speed high-torque burr that allows us to then start cutting and removing bone to straighten the toe. And then here we can see that we have now removed a section of bone that is allowing us to now straighten the toe. With our toe straightened, we then place a pin from the tip of the toe down to the base to allow us to maintain the straightened position that we were able to achieve. We verified with x-ray that the pin is in good position, and holding the toe as we would like. We will then typically cut and bend the pin to ensure that it does not catch on any clothes or other items, and that completes the procedure for the hammer toe correction. Now, we'll see what a hammer toe correction looks like when done in an open fashion. And we can see the dissection being done here across the top of the toe that will require us to move the tendon that moves the toe so that we have access to the bone and joint. This extensive dissection is one of the reasons that a known problem from hammer toe surgery is residual stiffness, because of how much the soft tissues have to be moved to gain access to this small joint and the bones underneath. And so here we can see our open incision next to our minimally invasive incision to appreciate the significant difference in the amount of dissection and soft tissue mobilization required. With the minimally invasive incision being so small, it's a much faster and typically smoother recovery for our patients, giving them the best possible outcome with the least amount of effort. Now, let's take a look at a minimally invasive calcaneal osteotomy. While minimally invasive techniques can be used for standalone procedures, they can also be used as an augment to much larger hindfoot reconstructions, such as we're going to see here. In this situation, we're going to be doing an osteotomy of the calcaneus, or a cut in the heel bone. We first begin by inserting guide wires into the heel bone to create borders, or to give us an outline of the cut we would like to create. And we can see here the outline of those borders that we're trying to create, and that's formed by this pin coming up and this other pin coming down, creating the triangle, or wedge, that we plan to remove. Once we've established that, we determine our starting point by trying to come close to the inferior apex of that triangle where we will make our keyhole incision, as you can see, visualized here, to be about the size of my blade. We then enter with our cutting burr, which is a high-torque, low-speed burr designed to protect our soft tissues but is strong enough to allow us to cut the bone. We first enter the bone, and then we start a process of reaming away everything that was between our two wires in that triangle. And as we ream, we remove the burr every once in a while, and place suction through the same hole to remove any bony fragments. This allows us to keep track of what we're doing, while ensuring that we're doing it safely and respecting the patient's adjacent soft tissues. So here we can see the wedge that we have created, and the bone that we have removed, represented by the clear space that you can see here, right in front of the wire. And we will continue to make that larger and larger as needed, until we have it large enough that we can now begin to mobilize our osteotomy site, and close down that wedge, so that you can see where it is now shortened and much smaller, as we are now able to move this posterior tuberosity anteriorly, thus changing the entire angle of the calcaneus. After we've shifted it forward, we then place guide wires to help hold position. We then place screws across our osteotomy site to bring it together, and close down the gap we have created, thus changing how the patient's foot meets the ground, how their Achilles meets the foot, and how the patient perceives their discomfort going forward with significant improvement of pain. This is our entry site for all of the hardware that we placed to adjust our calcaneal angle. And we can appreciate here the actual size of this incision being approximately one centimeter, which also matches the size of our surgical site, measuring approximately one centimeter, pictured here on the side of the foot. So we have just realigned the entire calcaneus, as well as this patient's ability for ambulation, through these two small one-centimeter incisions. Now let's compare that to what the open incision looks like. For the minimally invasive, we've taken it and shrunk it to one centimeter, where, on the open approach, you can appreciate that it is at least 4 to 5 centimeters, and requires me to move aside a significantly greater amount of tissue to get down onto the bone before we would even start making our cuts to remove a wedge and attempt to bring it forward. The need for increased visualization requires increased surgical time and dissection. One of the other differences between minimally invasive and open surgery is the requirement to hold the tissues open. The constant need to apply tension to the tissues to improve visualization also decreases the blood supply to those tissues during the approach and during the surgical procedure, which increases the chances of infection, wound healing complication, or post-operative wound breakdown due to poor blood supply. So here we can see the true difference between our minimally invasive incision versus our formal open incision, and the amount of dissection that is required, and the amount of soft tissue mobilization that is required. And that's why we're moving most of what we do here to our minimally invasive approaches, to help our patients recover faster, more comfortably, and get back to life more quickly. My colleagues and I here at Penn Medicine are constantly working to provide the latest surgical techniques to help our patients get back on their feet. To contact us about surgical options for your patient or to refer your patient to Penn Orthopaedics, call our dedicated referral line, or visit PennMedicine.org/Refer.

=== FILE: Neurosurgeon： Daniel Yoshor, MD, Penn Medicine [o3PmeHOE3h8].en.txt ===

Very early on, I could see that neurosurgery was right for me. I was always interested in how the mind works and I was attracted to the amazing field of neuroscience. And I also like helping people in a very direct way. Working with my hands and immediately fixing people with complicated problems. And I actually like the challenge of working with patients and families during the most important, most challenging moments in their lives. I'm Daniel Yoshor and I'm the Chair of Neurosurgery at Penn Medicine. I think it's really an honor and a privilege for us that in a very short amount of time we have to meet the patient and the family and quickly earn their confidence and show with sincerity that we are compassionate, we are knowledgeable, we are skilled, and we're going to give them the best possible care. I'm particularly focused on pituitary surgery and skull-based tumor surgery. A lot of those surgeries are being done using special cameras and instruments through the nose without an incision. And when a patient comes to the Penn Pituitary Center to see me, they're not just seeing me. They're usually seeing two or more other specialists and they receive the benefits of all this expertise all working together to help those patients. I think there really is a great joy when the surgery is working beautifully and you anticipate what's coming next. It is a little bit like a symphony, and it just becomes effortless and just a pleasure. And it's hard to convey that joy. That's why we love being in the operating room. There's no better feeling than that, than taking someone who is about to go blind, or lose the ability to function in many other ways, and restore them to good health quickly. Then the next day after surgery, they look at me and say, "Wow!  I can really see so much better. This is amazing."

=== FILE: New Advances in COPD Care ｜ Penn Precision Medicine [QVQhcL14kyo].en.txt ===

(soft music) - I once took care of a young patient who was being admitted to the ICU every month or two with renal failure or an infection. I discovered the real problem was that he didn't have bus tokens to get to the pharmacy for his medications. He was trading his tokens in exchange for rent. There are so many patients whose underlying reasons for coming to the hospital aren't on a doctor's official diagnosis list. This is especially true for patients living with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD. These patients often present to the hospital with shortness of breath, but may also be struggling with management of heart failure, limited access to medications, unstable housing, other severe unpalliated symptoms or other challenges in their lives. If we could identify such problems early, we could do something about them before a patient ends up in the hospital. The information needed to identify such problems usually isn't found in the official diagnosis list, but may be mentioned in the unstructured text of encounter notes that are written by clinicians. With support from the Penn Center for Precision Medicine, we are taking two important steps forward in the care of patients with COPD. First, we are interviewing patients and their caregivers to understand, in their own words, the physical, social, and economic barriers to good health. Second, we are using natural language processing, techniques that allow computers to analyze text data, to read the text of patients' clinical notes and identify these barriers. Finally, we will share these techniques and software tools widely with other health systems to identify patients with surmountable barriers to achieving good health. These tools will form the basis for future randomized clinical trials aimed at improving population health management for people living with COPD. I'm Dr. Gary Weissman, and this is Precision Medicine at Penn. (soft music)

=== FILE: New App Aims to Improve Outcomes for Lung Transplant Patients ｜ Penn Precision Medicine [rX7g2i88HvI].en.txt ===

(soft music) - Over 2300 patients undergo lung transplantation in the United States every year. With improvements in medical and surgical care, plus recent changes in lung allocation algorithms, older and sicker patients are prioritized for transplant each year. This can lead to increased length of stay, increased disability, and a development of frailty after lung transplantation, which can lead to a significant decline in health-related quality of life. Additionally, 60% of lung transplant patients are readmitted within 30 days after transplant. This can be physically and emotionally devastating for a patient who has been suffering for months or years prior to transplantation. What if there was a way to harness the power of our smartphones to improve physical function and prevent or reverse frailty after lung transplant? In collaboration with colleagues at the University of San Francisco, California and the medical application company AidCube, and with support from the Penn Center for Precision Medicine, we are utilizing a targeted, individualized, customizable physical therapy mobile health app to mitigate frailty, decrease hospital readmission rate, decrease healthcare expenditures, and improve health-related quality of life. I'm Dr. Joshua Diamond, and this is Precision Medicine at Penn.

=== FILE: Oral Bisphosphonates for treating Osteoporosis [8B_ZVaH0f9M].en.txt ===

my name is Christina Mitchell I'm one of the Physicians who sees patients in the pen bone Center and this video is a description about the oral bis phosphinates the bis phosphinates are one of the classes of osteoporosis medications and the oral bis phosphinates include actonel residronate Fosamax alendronate Boniva abandon and the last in the slide here is reclass zonic acid which is an ivis phosphinate these are medications that help to reduce the risk of bone loss and bone resorption in the slide here you'll notice that the osteoclast cells are the cells that degrade bone and they are followed by the osteoblast which deposit new bone the bis phosphinates the class of medications that we're speaking about today prevent the Osteo class from resorbing excess bone which effectively allow the osteoblast to catch up and deposit new bone the recommended dosing for these medications alendronate also known as Fosamax is typically given a 70 Mig once a week actinal can be given as 35 Mig weekly or 150 migr monthly we are not using Boniva as often as we have in the past because it does not have efficacy at the hip although it does work well at the spine the alendronate and residronate medications as I mentioned are oral bis phosphinates typically the course of therapy is about 3 to 5 years as I mentioned they are anti-resorptive medications they inhibit the action of the osteoclast and they are large nitrogen containing molecules which incorporate themselves into the bone matrix within the bone matrix they inhibit the osteoclast from binding to the Bone they actually block their physical attachment and those osteoclast that still manage to bind to the Bone if they ingest some of the bisphosphonate living therein will go through apoptosis or cell death the initial course of therapy is 5 years to be followed by a drug holiday so one benefit of these medications is that you do not need to take them indefinitely these medications are best taken first thing in the morning with an 8 o glass of water and then waiting about 30 minutes to eat it's recommended that you remain upright and not lie down for one hour after taking the medication to allow the medication to get all the way to the small intestine where it is absorbed and not to sit in the stomach where it can cause reflux or even esophagitis the these medications cannot be used if someone has kidney function below a certain level because of the possible adverse reaction of a rare side effect called osteon necrosis of the jaw it's recommended to receive regular dental care and to be up to date with the dentist prior to starting one of these medications please alert your doctor if you have a new symptom of dull or aching pain in your groin or thigh which could be another side effect representative of ayal atypical femur fracture

=== FILE: Osteoporosis  Myths and Facts [AP8Nz-iOyd8].en.txt ===

so in this section I wanted to go over some frequently asked questions that I get in clinic from my patients I get a lot of questions why are you asking me about my calcium intake you just did a blood test and my SERM calcium was normal isn't that a good representation of my calcium intake well the short answer is no your body under normal circumstances will do everything it can to maintain a normal serum calcium so if you're not getting enough calcium from your diet or supplements then you are going to be losing more calcium from your bones to maintain a normal serum calcium so that's why we always talk about adequate calcium intake on the opposite side if you're taking too much calcium you will lose that calcium in the urine and you will increase your risk of having kidney stones so please make sure to discuss with your doctor how much calcium you should be taking on a daily basis it's usually about 1,000 to 1200 Mill of calcium a day but in certain instances you might need to be taking more calcium if you're having problems with absorption or less calcium if you've had problems with kidney stones um a very commonly asked question is will my bone density ever improve or this is it well yes your bone mineral density can improve with therapy it can improve more so with some agents than others however stabilization of your bone mineral density or lack of significant decline in your bone mineral density which is something that we expect with age is a treatment success and that has been shown to be associated with decrease in risk of fractures if I am on osteoporosis medication do I still need to take calcium vitamin D and exercise absolutely I think about calcium and vitamin D as being the building blocks and the medications only work if you're taking enough calcium and vitamin D in addition we appreciate that osteoporosis is multifactorial and so when we're trying to address um osteoporosis and decreasing your risk of fractures we have to take it with a multifaceted approach so we do have to always talk about nutrition calcium vitamin D exercise fall prevention avoiding things that could negatively affect your bone quality like smoking excessive alcohol and caffeine intake everything has to be in moderation so excessive calcium supplementation is not recommended because that can increase risk of kidney stones and heavy lifting or high impact exercises can sometimes cause injury another commonly asked question is will carbonated or sparkling water negatively affect my bone quality well the data on carbonated beverages is really based on the dark carbonated beverages like Coca-Cola or sodas that have high phosphates in them and that can affect the absorption of calcium as of now we don't have any data to suggest that sparkling water or seltzer can negatively affect your bone quality if I exercise will my bone density improve well it might especially if you were very sedentary at Baseline however it's very unlikely that it will be enough to treat your osteoporosis is when we're prescribing medications for osteoporosis we want to prescribe something that we know can decrease your risk of breaking bones not just improve your bone density and exercise works really well in conjunction to medications will my hip or back pain improve with osteoporosis treatment and sadly the answer here is no osteoporosis is a silent disease and does not cause any pain and we don't expect that your pain will improve with osteoporosis medications osteoporosis medications can decrease your risk of having fractures and that could improve um your and that could decrease your risk of having future fractures and future pain but it will not help you with your current pain talk to your primary care doctor about the cause and discuss treatment for your pain do I have to be on osteoporosis medication for the rest of my life usually not usually medications we give them for courses so bis phosphinates are usually given for 3 to 5 years uh some of the daily the daily injections are given for two years um the monthly injections are given for one year and the infusions are usually three years um denosa which is Prolia it's given every six months and the duration of that is yet to be determined but we usually do not recommend medications lifelong but that doesn't mean that we're not addressing your osteoporosis at every visit and we're not discussing ways to decrease your risk of having a fracture at every visit and that doesn't mean that we don't talk about fall prevention with every visit so Lifestyle Changes nutrition calcium vitamin D uh exercise and fall prevention is an intervention that you will have to continue to do for the rest of your life but medications we give you courses of medications and then we give you drug holidays and then we can restart medications in the future thank you for your attention and I'm hopeful I was able to answer some of your questions

=== FILE: Osteoporosis Medications  differences between anti resorptive and osteo anabolic therapies [MahaB5Np4Eo].en.txt ===

so in this video I wanted to go over the different osteoporosis medications that we have and to go over how they work so what I usually tell my patients in clinic is that when someone develops osteoporosis what happens is that the amount of bone being removed is more than amount of bone being formed so bone removal happens by the osteoclasts and um we have medications that suppresses the amount of bone being removed we also have medications that can stimulate bone formation so I wanted to make that kind of Distinction uh at this during this educational video so most of the medications that we have for treatment of osteoporosis work by suppressing the amount of bone being removed so that class of medication is called anti-resorptive agents so that would include medications like bis phosphinates which are alendronate or known as Fosamax residronate or actinal or the infusion of zonic acid reclass denosumab which is peria is also an anti-resorptive agent which decreases the amount of bone being removed as well as estrogen rosmap calcitonin and ser um estrogen like medications as you can see here you can find Romo zmab on both both sections so Romo zmab is both an anti-resorptive agent as well as an osteoanabolic agent and it stimulates bone formation other agents that we have that stimulate bone formation are teriparatide and abaloparatide which are === FILE: Patient Visits： What to Expect During COVID-19 [gw1z5OTDbeU].en.txt ===

A lot has changed here at Penn Medicine since the outbreak of COVID-19. As we begin to return to normal, we want to let you know what we’re doing to ensure patient and staff safety, and what you can expect when you arrive for an appointment. First, we’ve enabled Patient Pre Check-In on the myPennMedicine portal in order to minimize time spent in our facilities. Just login, and with a few quick clicks, our clinical team will know you’re ready to arrive for your scheduled appointment. When you enter the building, you’ll notice that staff and patient entrances are now separate to better control traffic through doors. There will also be contactless temperature screenings at all entrances, so only those without COVID-19 symptoms will be allowed inside. As always, our greeters will be there to help you find your way, and you’ll notice they are wearing masks, and standing at least 6 feet apart from others. For those of you taking an elevator to get to your appointment, there will be limits to how many people can enter at one time. Frequently touched surfaces like elevator buttons are being constantly wiped down, and our cleaning staff are regularly disinfecting all areas of our facilities in order to halt the spread of germs. Across Penn Medicine’s locations, you’ll find hand sanitizing stations, so no matter what your route is, you’ll have many opportunities to disinfect along the way. When you arrive at check-in areas, you’ll notice plexiglass separators and rearranged waiting rooms, all designed with your safety in mind. Our providers will be wearing masks at all times, and remain at a safe distance while discussing your care. If your care requires a physical exam, be assured that our providers will be sanitizing and wearing all required protective equipment - for your safety, and theirs. We’ve also made some changes to our common areas and cafeterias to ensure a safe, relaxing experience between appointments, without needing to leave the building. And if you’re picking up prescriptions at our pharmacy, you’ll see that dividers have been put in place to allow for a contactless experience. We understand this is not an easy time, and we’re here to help you every step of the way. At Penn Medicine, our top priority is providing world-class patient care in a safe and comfortable environment, for you and your loved ones.

Welcome to the podcast series from the specialists at Penn Medicine. I'm Melanie Cole and today we're discussing the limb preservation program at Penn Medicine. Joining me is Dr. Julia Glasser. She's a vascular surgeon and an assistant professor of clinical surgery at Penn Medicine. Dr. Glasser, it's a pleasure to have you with us today. As we get into this topic, can you tell us a little bit about the current state of diabetes and how the lower extremity amputation is an unfortunate and often avoidable squella of complicated diabetes? Tell us a little bit about critical limb eskeeia and who it affects. Sure. And thanks so much for having me today. This is a really important topic and I think affects a lot of people across the country and particularly a lot of people in Philadelphia, which is why it's so important to get the word out there about the conditions that lead to this and also what we're doing here at Penn to prevent amputation. You're absolutely right. People who have particularly poorly controlled diabetes for a long time can have peripheral vascular disease. Essentially, high blood sugar over a long period of time damages the blood vessels, both large blood vessels as well as small blood vessels. That can make people more likely to develop wounds and at the same time, the damage to the blood vessels prevents enough blood flow from getting to the wounds to help people heal them. Critical limb eskeeia means the endstages of what's known as peripheral arterial disease. Peripheral arterial disease refers to blockages in the blood vessels. It tends to affect smokers. It affects men more often than women and it also affects people with endstage renal disease especially folks on diialysis and people with diabetes. Diabetes and pad as we call it are linked pretty tightly. Critical limb eskeemia affects people with poorly controlled diabetes and can lead to amputation. And that's really why we put this program together to help prevent amputation in these folks who are unfortunately susceptible to these complications. Everything from that all the way to on the other end of the spectrum minimally invasive endovvascular techniques using the latest technology in stenting drugcoded stenting angoplasty atherctomy all those sorts of things. Yeah, historically standard treatment was open bypass. And the trouble with open bypass was that if your heart wasn't working well or lungs, you weren't really a candidate for open bypass. And so endovvascular treatment has allowed us to do a lot more for a whole lot more people. It's allowed us to improve profusion in a whole lot more people who traditionally wouldn't have been candidates for open bypass. And if you look at data across the country, meta analyses have shown that the rate of open bypass has gone down while the rate of endovvascular interventions has gone up. And that's actually been associated with a decrease in the number of amputations. If you look across the country, we haven't quite seen this effect in diabetics just yet. Sometimes they need help from endocrinology. Sometimes they need help from infectious disease. === FILE: Penn Medicine Clinical Simulation Center [waq2KJdZP50].en.txt ===

Exceptional healthcare begins with exceptional training. At the Pen Medicine Clinical Simulation Center, clinicians are acquiring the skills and education they need to provide safer care and improve clinical outcomes. Opened in 2008, the state-of-the-art simulation center serves as a valuable training ground for thousands of Penn students, residents, and attending physicians, nurses, and ancillary healthcare staff from around the world. Within the 22,000q ft simulation center, the most advanced and diverse of its kind in the world, individuals enjoy a safe, risk-free environment in which to learn and practice procedures, appropriately respond to a variety of clinical situations, and hone their communication skills. At the heart of the center are six rooms that simulate different settings and scenarios. Each room is equipped with a lifelike mannequin that can respond physiologically like a real patient. A comprehensive audiovisisual system records all training in each room for future review either locally or remotely. In these six simulation rooms, teams of health care professionals are presented with various clinical scenarios. 5-year-old gentleman for a left ranging from a complicated birth to a fire in the operating room. Fire in the arts. Get the drapes down. Get the drapes down. Call collaboratively. The team must resolve each challenge or achieve goal-directed therapy. The simulation center features 12 patient exam rooms used to assess and polish the clinical ability, communication skills, and professionalism of both medical students and seasoned healthcare professionals alike. The cent's MI surgical skill suite houses multiple virtual reality task trainers for practicing procedures such as upper and lower endoscopy, robotic surgery, and various vascular procedures. Rounding out the simulation center is a multi-sklls lab for basic skills training using lowfidelity trainers such as central line, foley catheter, arterial line, and more. While owned and operated by Penn Medicine, the simulation center is available for outside medical professionals, students, and training groups who want to take advantage of its resources. As an American Heart Association approved training site, the simulation center also offers advanced cardiac life support and basic cardiac life support training for clinical professionals. The goal of the simulation center is to provide current and future medical personnel with a simulated learning environment that translates into improved education, greater safety, and better outcomes for all of our patients. To learn more about the Pen Medicine Clinical Simulation Center, or to learn how you can support the center, call us or visit our website.
