=== FILE: Penn Medicine's AERD Center [x6hJLpvPYUs].en.txt ===

Welcome to the podcast series from the specialists at Penn Medicine. I'm Melanie Cole and join us as we discuss the pen aspirin exacerbated respiratory disease or AERD center. Joining me in this panel are Dr. John Boso. He's a clinical professor and serves as the medical director of the AERD center at pen odilarangology head and neck surgery. and he's the director of Odellarangology allergy clinic at Penn Medicine and Dr. Nathan Adapa he's an associate professor in the department of odilarangology and the surgical director of the AERD center at Penn ottoarangology head and neck surgery gentlemen I'm so glad to have you join us today and Dr. Baso, before we get into this topic, can you describe your personal history with aspirin exacerbated respiratory disease or AERD? It all started when I was a fellow in my final leg of training. I was out at Scripps' clinic in California and we were the Sentinel site where we were studying this condition and my mentors were at that time studying the mechanism of the disease. We were getting patients from all over the country to come in to try out a therapy which was basically to desensitize patients to aspirin and this was something that was serendipitously discovered and I was fortunate enough to learn the technique at an early time where really not too much was known about this condition. Thank you for that. So Dr. Adapa, why don't you tell for other providers that may not know what is AERD? So ARD or as you mentioned as exacerbated respiratory disease is a progressive disease process. The patients manifest with chronic sinocitis with nasal polyps asthma and they have a sensitivity to NSAIDs. Initially was described as essentially it's any any NSAID. So it's a progressive disease that can develop at any age typically past puberty but most commonly in patients in their 30s and 40s where initially they'll develop either the nasal complaints or the asthma complaints and then over the next few years develop the rest of this triad from a odolarangologist perspective it's the most severe type of chronic sinocitis nasal palposis. So from our end of things, this is a very problematic disease to treat because of the severity. And in addition, these patients really end up not getting their diagnosis early enough because a lot of practitioners don't put the pieces together. One person might see them for their sinuses, one person might see them for their asthma, and when they develop an allergic reaction to an NSAID, they may not really think it's part of the syndrome, and they may end up in an emergency room or something like that for the reaction, but no one puts the pieces together that this is one syndrome. How interesting. So then, Dr. Baso, how is it diagnosed and by whom? Tell us about some of those symptoms of it and who might notice them. Is this for primary care providers? Who would notice? Well, anyone really can notice if they take a good history. So, patients who develop adult onset chronic rhinocyitis with nasal polyps, asthma, and respiratory reactions to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs including aspirin would be the patients that we would suspect would have this condition. Usually if they have at least two bonafide reactions or one serious reaction to aspirin or NSAIDs plus the polyps sinusitis and asthma that certainly should be enough in most cases to make the diagnosis. Now the respiratory reactions can be as mild as sneezing, nasal congestion, nasal blockage, runny nose, but most of the time they involve acute bronco spasm, wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and very rarely skin manifestations such as flushing and hives and and even more rare drops in blood pressure, elevated pulse rates. Putting the whole package together does require a good history. Now a lot of patients will not give you a perfect history or you may not have it or they may not even be taking uh medication in the NSET family. So you may not know what the diagnosis is when it's not clear. The definitive gold standard is to do what's called an aspirin challenge where we bring a patient in uh withhold any medications that may have suppressive effects on reactions such as antihistamines and give gradually increasing doses of aspirin in a supervised setting and of course if a patient has any reactions immediately stop the challenge and treat them and confirm the diagnosis. There is no blood test or skin test or urine test that really is definitively accurate. We wish there was that would give us a clear-cut answer as to whether this patient has the syndrome. So, we rely on a good history or an aspirin challenge when the history is not clear-cut. And I'd like to add the other part for providers to think about is often you'll ask a patient who has asthma and nasal polyps, do you have a reaction to NSAIDs or aspin products? and they'll quickly say no. And you really have to interrogate that a little further because there's a lot of patients they instinctually say no. So you really want to interrogate whether this patient has taken these products recently as they're developing this syndrome or not because if the answer is no, you still haven't completely ruled it out. And then the other issue is as I think we're highlighting here, this is a progressive disease process. You don't wake up one day where you have all three aspects of the syndrome. Rather, they're going to develop over several years. And so you may catch a patient who has new onset asthma and nasal polyps, but they may not have developed that aspirin component yet. So you still want to think about that in the back of your mind. That's a patient who's newly diagnosed. This is such an interesting topic and really important information for providers. Thank you both for that diagnosis and history information. So important. Now, Dr. Adapa tell us how the treatment has now evolved and what's the latest treatment protocol at pen medicine. So the treatment protocol in general is complete sinus surgery followed by aspirin desensation. Now this sounds fairly straightforward and I will tell you before Dr. boss came to Penn Medicine. He was a couple hours away in Nyak, New York. And we'd identified these ARD patients where I would see them or my partner Jim Palmer. We would see them, we would treat them, and then we'd send them over to NYAK, New York to get the aspirin desensation. Where we really evolved in a big way was when we were able to get John over to Penn with us where we really could do coordinated care. So, it's not just surgery. It's making sure you do the thorough surgery. And that surgery really means meticulous clean out of every area of the sinuses. And not everybody has the expertise or the equipment to safely do these type of procedures. And once they're cleaned out, then in a coordinated fashion, you need to immediately get them into that desensation before any polyps grow back. If there's a delay in care or there's not coordinated care and some of these polyps start growing back, then the aspirin desensation part of this does not work nearly as well. So that really has been a big boon for us and how we've been getting uh much better results. When John got here, our results improved that much further just for our coordinated center here. Yeah. So the ribs as they become the costal cartilage on the anterior chest have multiple cartilage to cartilage junctions that are very thin and very easy to break. And in the majority of patients that I see most of whom are very young healthy and athletic people there's a single cartilage junction that's broken. === FILE: Penn Medicine's Living Liver Donation Program [3szjpwU-Vf8].en.txt ===

Welcome to the Penn Transplant Institute Center for Living Donation. Today we're going to give you an overview of living liver donation and what you should know as a potential donor. We're very excited that you're interested in this prospect to help people who need liver transplantation and want to make sure that you are well informed along this journey. Living liver donor transplantation is a life-saving measure for people with endstage liver disease. We also believe that it is a better alternative for most transplant candidates. Organ allocation regulations are ever changing and the wait time for a deceased donor organ can be challenging and lengthy currently and for the foreseeable future. For this reason, patients are asked to advocate for themselves to find a living liver donor to expedite this process. To begin, let's review some of the issues pertaining to confidentiality and disclaimers. It is important to realize that a living liver donor may opt out at any time and for any reason up till general anesthesia is administered. Your health information as a donor is confidential and separate from the recipient's health record. The health record is also confidential and is protected under privacy laws. Therefore, all communication is strictly confidential. Recipients might be informed that there is a donor in evaluation, if a donor has been approved, or if there are no potential living donors to consider at a given point in time. You can share as much or as little as you want regarding your health information or motivations with your recipient, but we cannot and will not share the details of your health record with the intended recipient. Every donor underos a psychosocial assessment and reviews risk criteria for certain illnesses and infectious diseases such as HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C in accordance with the US federal policy. It is a federal crime to sell or purchase human organs, and you cannot receive anything of valuable consideration in exchange for donation. Although rare, donation could have an impact on obtaining health, life, or disability insurance in the future. If you feel any pressure in donating or coercion to donate, please make our team aware immediately. There are alternatives to living donation for both donors and recipients. As a donor, you always have the option to change your mind. Being a living liver donor is a completely voluntary act on your part. On the recipient side, the recipients physicians may choose to pursue medical management. The recipient may undergo a deceased donor transplant or recipients might be listed at multiple centers to improve their odds of being transplanted. Potentially, they could explore alternate living donor options. Let's talk about your living donor team. The living donor team follows a multiddisciplinary approach to care. All discussions and decisions are made with you, the donor, as our central focus of this process. Members of the living donor team include the living donor surgeon, the medical liver specialist known as a hepatologist, and the living donor advanced practice provider like a physician assistant or nurse practitioner. These individuals all work together to review your motivations to be a donor, as well as your medical, surgical, social, and family history. They also set expectations for the medical and surgical evaluation, the surgery, and the post-operative period, and discuss the risks of the living donor surgery from their perspective. They'll also determine if any additional individualized testing or other consults are needed. You may be asked to see a cardiologist to ensure that your heart is healthy enough for this type of surgery. The social worker will review your financial information and social support and can provide information regarding certain assistance programs that are available to you as a living donor. The psychiatrist will assess your mental health history and your coping mechanisms. The nutritionist will assess whether you require weight loss prior to donation. The pharmacist will review your medications and will let you know if any need to be temporarily stopped in preparation for surgery. Lastly, the financial coordinator will work to prevent charges associated with living donation from being build to the donor. An independent living donor advocate or ILDA will assist you in this journey. The independent living donor advocate role is required for all living donor programs in all transplant centers in the United States. The donor advocate works independently but collaboratively with the living donor team. The sole focus of the living donor advocate is to look after the interests of the donor and support the donor through the entire process. The independent living donor advocate will assist the donor with education and will help the donor understand relevant information like the consent process, the evaluation process, the surgical procedure, the medical, psychosocial and financial risks, and the important of and commitment to postdonation followup. Most of all, the independent living donor advocate works to ensure that a donor's decisions are respected and ensures the decision is informed, free from pressure by the recipient, family, or friends, and without financial compensation or manipulation. The living donor nurse coordinator is your clinical resource coordinator who screens donor inquiries, escalates, and communicates information between you and the rest of the donor team. The coordinator facilitates the evaluation process and educates the donor and their families in all phases of care. The coordinator will also prepare the donor for surgery and will ensure that the case is coordinated with the recipient team. Let's discuss the living donor process. At this point, you are already well into the referral process. You completed the online screening form at penransplant.donorscreen.org. This screening is done in partnership with the National Kidney Registry or NKR. You've had your screening labs drawn and based on those results, you have been moved forward and completed a telephone screening with the Independent Living Donor Advocate. Our screening criteria focuses on the following points. The donor must be in very good health. The donor should be between the ages of 21 and 50, but slightly older or slightly younger donors may be considered on a case-byase basis. The donor is ideally blood type compatible with the recipient though may be eligible to participate in a process called liver paired donation if not. The donor should not be significantly overweight meaning the donor should have a body mass index or BMI under 28. The donor must have health insurance and should have a primary care physician. You may request a copy of our donor and or recipient selection criteria by contacting us once you have completed viewing this video. The donor evaluation process can take several weeks to months to complete. You will be asked to come to our center two to three separate times for appointments and testing. During that time frame, you will have a medical evaluation, a surgical evaluation, a psychosocial evaluation with social work and/or psychiatry and meet the independent living donor advocate. You will also have diagnostic tests like blood work and imaging. We will ask you to provide us with age appropriate screening tests done as part of your own health maintenance such as a mammogram, hapsmear, or colonoscopy depending on your age. You may also need to meet other living donor team members and specialists if indicated like infectious disease, hematology or pulmonology. Once all testing and consults have been completed, the team will meet to discuss your care. At each point in the evaluation process, your results will be made available to you and explained to you. If you are declined as a living donor, that means the team feels that living donation is not a safe option for you. The most common reasons individuals are declined are insufficient liver volume in incompatible liver anatomy, medical concerns that are found in evaluation, or psychosocial concerns. It is also possible that you could be declined for reasons associated with the intended recipient, for example, a change in the recipient's health status. The team may also decide that additional testing is needed to determine whether you can be approved. If this is the case, your donor coordinator will notify you and explain what is needed and field any questions you may have. If you're approved for donation, this means that the team has discussed your case thoroughly and feels that all of the testing results and necessary consultations are complete and reassuring with no additional items needed. If you are approved, you will be given time to reflect on your decision before we notify the recipient team. Once you have made your decision, the recipient team will not be notified and a date for surgery will be identified. The date will be suitable for the donor, the recipient and the transplant team. The surgery is timed so that all members of the surgical team are present. In some cases, a potential liver donor may not be a suitable match for their intended recipient for reasons including blood type, size, anatomy, or age. In these instances, you may still be able to help your recipient through liver pair donation. With liver pair donation, we try to find another donor and recipient pair at our center to participate in a swap or exchange so that your intended recipient ultimately gets a liver transplant. If another match or pair is identified, you would donate portion a portion of your liver to the other recipient while their donor would donate a portion of their liver to your recipient. In some cases, non-directed liver donors or donors without an intended recipient may be integrated into liver paired donation. The benefit is that it can lead to two life-saving transplants instead of one. The donor evaluation process is typically very similar with liver paired donation. However, it may take longer to find a match and schedule surgery. We will now discuss the transplant surgery process. Special circumstances exist for distance donors and international donors that require them to stay local to our center or within a commutable distance for a period of time after surgery. If you are a distance or international donor, this will be discussed with you at length during your evaluation process to allow you to prepare. After approval and prior to surgery, you will have a pre-operative office visit with the surgical team. This pre-operative visit is with the transplant surgeon and members of the surgical team one to two weeks prior to surgery so that we can review the details and logistics that are involved with the surgery itself. We encourage you to eat a healthy, well- balanced diet, exercise routinely, including cardio exercise, and continue to maintain or potentially even lose weight if you have been asked to do so. The pre-operative visit may require several hours to meet with the surgical team, sign surgical consent forms, and have preop blood work drawn. At the visit, we will also review pre-procedure information, and discuss the day-to-day of what your hospital's stay and recovery will be like. On the day of the surgery, you will arrive at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania Clifton Center early in the morning, usually around 6:00 or 7 a.m. You and the recipient will be in separate operating rooms side by side. The donor will generally go into the operating room 1 to 2 hours before the recipient, though there may be certain circumstances in which the recipient surgery will begin first. or the donor. The anesthesia team will administer medication into the spinal area similar to an epidural to help with abdominal pain control after surgery. Then the anesthesia team administers medication to put you to sleep. After you are asleep, there will be a series of monitoring devices and IVs placed like an IV in the neck called a central line, an IV in the wrist called an arterial line which measures blood pressure, a urinary catheter to drain urine from the bladder during the surgery, and a thin plastic tube that goes down the nose into the stomach to drain it called the nasogastric tube. Other external monitoring sensors like EKG leads will be placed on you. The surgical procedure itself takes about 6 hours once the incision is made, though the duration can vary. At any point during the operation, if we feel that it's not safe to proceed for your safety or for recipient safety, the surgery will be stopped. During the surgery, your designated support person will receive text updates in the waiting room, and the living donor nurse coordinator will keep your support person updated on how things are proceeding in the operating room. It's important to remember that you may change your mind and notify the team that you do not wish to proceed with surgery up until the point of general anesthesia. Prior to reviewing the details of surgery, let's discuss some basic information about the liver. The liver is responsible for many metabolic needs of the body and makes proteins that help the blood to clot. The liver is located in the upper portion of the abdomen above the belly button on the right side and is protected by the rib cage. The liver is a large segmented organ that can be split without harm to the donor. Depending on which lobe or section of the liver is donated, it is possible that the surgeons will need to remove your gallbladder during surgery. After surgery, the donor and recipients livers will grow in size to meet the body's needs. The majority of liver regeneration occurs within the first 3 months after donation. As mentioned, the surgeries for the donor and the recipient are performed in two adjacent operating rooms. We typically bring the donor to the operating room before the recipient surgery starts. Once we ensure that everything is progressing well with the donor's surgery, then we bring the recipient to the operating room as well. There are certain circumstances in which we may begin the recipient surgery. First, the donor's surgery is started laparoscopically using a minimally invasive approach. Three small 1 to 2 cm incisions are made. One on the right side of the abdomen and two in the midline of the abdomen. Through these small incisions, the surgeons will introduce surgical tools and air is placed within the abdomen to temporary temporarily lift the abdominal wall off of the abdominal organs. During the first phase of the surgery, the liver is mobilized from the rib cage and from attachments so that the surgeon can divide the liver. During the second phase of the surgery, a larger linear incision is made from the bottom of the breast bone to the belly button so that the surgeon has better visibility and access to divide the liver and remove the portion that will be donated to the recipient. During the surgery, an X-ray called a collangiogram will be performed to visualize bile ducts that run through the liver. This gives the surgeon a road map of the bile duct anatomy. The surgeon will divide the liver into two pieces with very careful attention to the bile ducts and blood vessels. The percent of the liver tissue removed varies depending on both the donor and the recipient size and needs. If you are donating the right lobe of the liver to an adult, up to 70% of the liver may be removed. Whether you are donating the left lateral segment of the liver, the left lobe of the liver, or the right lobe of the liver, the incisions should ultimately appear as small 1 to 2 cm laparoscopic incisions on the right side of the abdomen and a long linear midline incision from below the breast bone to the belly button. If you are donating the right lobe of the liver, the surgeon will remove the gallbladder to gain better access to the liver. If the left lobe or left lateral segment is selected for donation, you may not have to have your gallbladder removed. The gallbladder is not an essential organ and you may have heard of other people having their gallbladder removed for reasons like gallstones. Once the donation surgery is finished, the breathing tube will be removed and you will be transported to the posttop anesthesia care unit called the PACU. When you wake up, the IV in the neck, in the wrist, the nasogastric tube, the urinary catheter, and an abdominal drain will be in place. You will be observed in the post anesthesia care unit to ensure that your breathing is stable, pain management is adequate, and that nausea is controlled. Next, you will be transferred to the surgical intensive care unit for very close observation and monitoring for the first 24 hours or so after surgery. During this first 24 hours, your inpatient care team will start to remove the nasogastric tube, urinary catheter, and IV from the neck and wrist when appropriate to do so. If everything is progressing well in the ICU, you'll be transferred down the hall to the inpatient transplant unit, which is staffed by physicians, surgeons, surgical fellows, advanced practice providers, and nurses who are well trained in caring for both transplant donors and recipients. The inpatient hospital stay will be approximately 5 to 7 days with the focus being on pain control, advancing your diet, and making sure that you feel stable walking, using the bathroom, and caring for yourself. Our goal is for donors to be out of bed on the first postoperative day, walking every day in the hospital room and hallway. Once the nasogastric tube is removed, the team can offer you clear fluids to drink, and if that is going well, we can advance your diet further. We'll transition you from IV pain medications to oral pain medications, including Tylenol and ibuprofen. Oral opioid pain medication is available as needed, but we encourage you to optimize non-narcotic pain control options when possible. Most patients have the abdominal drain removed prior to hospital discharge, but for some it may be necessary to keep it in place a few additional days. The team will encourage you to walk and take deep breaths with a tool called the incentive sperometer to keep your lungs inflated. This reduces your risk for pneumonia and collapsed lung tissue called adalcttois. After surgery, we recommend that you do not lift, push, or pull anything heavier than 10 lbs or roughly a gallon of milk for the first 6 weeks to give your abdomen time to heal and reduce your risk of developing a hernia. We encourage you to walk daily and maintain your strength and expedite your recovery. You may go up and downstairs if you feel able to. You may shower 48 hours after surgery, but we do not want you to submerge in any baths, pools, or hot tubs until the incisions are fully healed. This is usually around 6 weeks after surgery. We do not want you to drive for the first 4 weeks after surgery, or until cleared by your surgical team. For your safety, we need to make sure that your pain is well controlled, the anesthesia has fully worn off, and that you are no longer taking opioid pain medications before driving again. Most donors return to work about 6 to 8 weeks after surgery. But in rare instances, you may need as long as 3 months to recover if your job requires strenuous activity or heavy lifting. A small percentage of donors may experience some shifts in their normal mood, anxiety, depression, or change in their sense of body image. Our social worker and transplant psychiatrists are supportive resources to help you along your donation journey and connect you with services and support groups that can help. As discussed earlier, postsurgical followup is extremely important for your safety. We are required to see you at very specific time points and report our findings to our regulatory agencies. You will see your surgical team after hospital discharge for a posttop follow-up visit at approximately 2, 4, and 6 weeks after surgery. If everything is proceeding as expected, you'll come back to our center 3 months after surgery for a follow-up visit with the hepatology team. If you are a right lobe donor, you will have an MRI of the abdomen at this time to assess regeneration of the liver. You will also have a visit with the hepatology team at 6 months postoperatively, which can be done via tele medicine. Your living donor nurse coordinator will check in by phone with you at 1 and 2 years after donation. At each of these time points, you will have lab work done and a check of your weight. lab work for the six-month, one-year, and two-year marks can be done at a pen lab or a Quest lab. Donor safety is our number one priority. With that in mind, it is important to also recognize that liver donation is a major surgery and we must review the potential risks associated with it. If you progress through the donation process and are scheduled for surgery, we will review the surgical process and risks in great detail with you and make sure to address any questions or concerns you may have. While these potential risks and complications are possible, they are very rare events and we are proud that our program's complication rate is very, very low for our donors. Minor risks typically require a small amount of intervention or no treatment at all. And these are conditions like acid reflux, change in your bowel habits, or swelling of the ankles. Muscularkeeletal aches and pains, urinary retention, or temporary numbness or tingling in your arms or legs due to surgical positioning are also possible and typically get better with time. Minor infections like a skin infection, pneumonia, or urinary tract infection due to a urinary catheter are possible and can be treated with antibiotics. Delayed wound healing requiring wound care can occur. Moderate risks include bile leak, blood clot in the legs or lungs, pneumothorax or collapsed lung or hernia. Throughout the liver, there are small channels called bile ducts which carry bile that the liver makes. When the liver is split into two pieces, the exposed bile ducts that are on the cut surface are carefully evaluated and tied off. There is still a small chance that one of these ducts may leak and often times this is detected on the color of the fluid in the abdominal drain that is placed while you are in the hospital. In most instances, a bile leak will resolve on its own. In rare instances, a special endoscopy procedure may be needed to be performed using a scope to reach the bile duct to place a small plastic tube in the bile duct to redirect flow. As previously discussed, any surgery and hospitalization increases your risk of developing a blood clot in the legs or lungs. For this reason, we give you a lowd dose blood thinner injection in the hospital and encourage walking early on to reduce risk. Collapsed lung or pneumthorax is rare but can occur relative to the placement of the large IV in the neck called the central line. Hernas are out pouchings of the bowel through an area of weakness in the abdominal wall and these can occur at any time there is abdominal surgery. These are very rare and occur infrequently. As with any major surgery, there's always a risk of acute liver failure or even death. Since the start of liver living donation in 1988, there have been a small number of reported donor deaths across the country. However, we have not had any living liver donor deaths here at the University of Pennsylvania. As you continue to follow and optimize your health after surgery, it is important for your team to know about any new medical diagnoses that you might receive from any other medical care providers. Some medical conditions are reportable from a regulatory standpoint after donation and we may be required to draw or store blood samples from donors for up to 10 years after donation. This is for the purpose of screening for infectious diseases and investigating potentially donor- derived diseases transmitted to the recipient. There are also some conditions that develop after donation that we need to report to the recipient transplant center as they could affect the health of the recipient. Examples of these conditions include any infectious disease or cancer that is discovered during the first 2 years of post-operative care. If you report any of these conditions, the following actions may be required. The recipient may be notified. We may need to report to local, state, or federal public health authorities as required by law. Or we may need to notify the recipient transplant center if it's outside of Penn. We may also need to notify the OPN improving safety portal, which is a national donor database. Importantly, if your doctor suspects that a health issue has developed related to your donation, please notify your living donor coordinator as soon as possible so that we can coordinate the clinical evaluation here at Then Regarding financial information and billing, the recipient's insurance usually covers your medical expenses, but some insurance carriers may have special requirements to cover living donors. The recipient's insurance does not cover expenses such as lost wages or travel expenses. For those who qualify, there are government assistance grants and programs like donor shield to help cover expenses for donors who qualify. Our social worker will review these resources with you and guide you through your options. To enhance convenience and offset travel costs, some patients living beyond a 25m radius to the hospital elect to stay at the Clyde F. Barker Transplant House in Philadelphia. The Barker House is a pen guest house for donors, transplant recipients, and caregivers who would like to stay close to the hospital before or after surgery for some portion of time. For more information on the Barker House, you can visit the website listed here. National and center specific surgical outcome data is available for your review at www.srtr.org. We encourage you to review this data. Our team is available to answer any questions you may have regarding donor or recipient outcomes at Penn. Our transplant center always has a transplant surgeon, hepatologist, transplant coordinator, and advanced practice provider on call 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. They are available to receive organ offers, recover deceased donor organs, perform transplant surgeries, and address urgent clinical needs of our patients. If there is a change in our ability to provide this coverage, we will notify you. If there is a local or regional emergency that impacts our ability to provide transplant care, we will use the available resources to notify you and identify a local or regional center that will help transfer your care. The United Network for Organ Sharing, known as UNOS, is a federal agency that oversees organ donation and transplant for all organs in the United States. This organization keeps the national patient waiting list for organ transplants. Lastly, UNOS and CMS require that transplants be provided in a Medicare approved transplant center to ensure the recipient's ability to have imunosuppression medication paid for by Medicare. In its place in cancer therapy and prostate cancer therapy, brachi is important for the treatment of men with clinically localized intact prostate cancer, meaning that these patients still have their prostate gland intact. And breaky therapy can be used really for all patients with intact prostate cancer who don't have contraindications to anesthesia or they don't have other factors that they would not be able to receive the treatment or they don't have significant lower urinary tract symptoms and there are a few different types correct can you speak a little bit about the different types that you might look to there are two major types of prostate breakchie therapy the first is permanent seed implantation or LDR or lowd dose rate breakchie therapy And the other is highd dose rate breakchie therapy or temporary implantation. Permanent seat implantation has been around for a long time. It's been very well studied. And this involves the implantation in a single outpatient session anywhere from 45 minutes to 2 hours under general anesthesia placing anywhere from about 50 to 100 seeds directly into the prostate gland. In this fashion, it's convenient because it's a single outpatient session. Some of the challenges though are patients are radioactive for potentially up to 3 months while those seeds decay and deliver the treatment dose to the patients and some men would prefer not to be that way. The service that we'll be offering at pen medicine highdose rate therapy is delivered in a slightly different way. We place hollow needles inside the prostate again while the patient is under general anesthesia and then using ultrasound based planning we deliver the treatment while the patient is asleep. Then we remove the needles. The patient wakes up with no radioactivity inside of them and no radioactivity that goes home. So it offers some slight differences. We use real-time ultrasound planning and there is no radioactivity when the patient goes home. So then is breaky therapy more convenient than external beam radiation? Can you compare and contrast a little for us? Sure. So external beam radiation therapy is typically delivered with IMRT or intensity modulated radiation therapy or it can be delivered with proton therapy. The number of treatments for each of those types of therapies is generally the same potentially on the order of up to 44 treatments and for what we call moderately hypofractionated regimens about 28 treatments or maybe four to 5 weeks. Breaky therapy can be considered more convenient in that it reduces the total number of treatment visits or total episodes of treatment compared to external beam radiation. When breakchie therapy is used alone, it can be delivered in a single treatment, say with permanent seeds. When it's used in high dose just as a treatment as a monotherapy, it can be delivered in two outpatient sessions. So that affords the patients a significant amount of convenience because it's fewer treatments. There's also no downtime. Men can return to work the next day. When used in combination, it can reduce the total number of treatments as well. So men who receive uh breakchie therapy as part of their radiation package, they might receive one breakchie therapy session and that might be followed by anywhere from 16 to 25 outpatient sessions. So breaky therapy can significantly reduce the overall amount of treatment and downtime and kind of lifestyle interference in the treatment of prostate cancer. Dr. Tonk can you speak about when breaky therapy might be used alone as primary first line versus as a second line or adgiant therapy? Okay, great. So I'll focus mostly on high dose rate breaky therapy. Another advantage of high dose rate breaky therapy is that involves what we call superior conformality compared to seed implantation. mean that we have the ability to control the dose and stay off of organs like the rectum, bladder, and urethra a little bit better than we've ever been able to. In terms of where this comes into their treatment, men with clinically localized prostate cancer who do not have significant lower urinary tract symptoms such as getting up in the middle of the night many times or rushing to the bathroom or other irritative urinary symptoms are eligible to receive monotherapy or breakchie therapy alone. as curative treatment in the first line and this is generally done in two outpatient sessions. For men with more advanced disease for example unfavorable intermediate risk prostate cancer or high-risisk prostate cancer that is Gleason 8 or T3 with say extra capsular extension or seminal vesicle invasion. Really the preferred approach is to do high dose rate breaky therapy combined with external beam radiation in the first line setting. This is also often combined with androgen deprivation therapy or hormone therapy. The reason that the combination approach is favored is that men would need treatment to the pelvis to the pelvic lymph nodes which the external beam radiation would do. And then the breaky therapy offers us the ability to deliver ultra high doses to the intact prostate cancer. But in addition, we can target lesions that have extra capsular extension or seminal vesicle invasion that we previously were really never able to target effectively. So those are the types of patients that are eligible in the first line setting. We don't use this in the adgiant setting after the prostate comes out. So there's no role for breakchie therapy after the prostate is removed. But there is a role for breakchie therapy for patients who have what we call radio recurrent prostate cancer. And these are men who've had external beam radiation in the past and their prostate cancer has recurred again inside the prostate. we can treat those patients with breakchie therapy effectively and offer them curative intent treatment while also being able to spare organs like the bladder, urethra and rectum from significant side effects. Can you speak a little bit about radiation safety or exposure issues and when might the use of breaky therapy be limited by other factors or comorbid conditions? So let's do the the second half of your question first. When would you not want to do this or who would not be the ideal candidate? Patients who may not be the optimal candidate for breakchie therapy are patients with significant lower urinary tract symptoms, meaning irritative urinary symptoms. They might not be ideal. Patients who do not have a rectum, say for prior surgery around the rectum, uh we can't perform this because we can't see the prostate gland. Patients who are unable to receive general anesthesia because our practice does this under general anesthesia would not be able to receive this either. And then there's some soft contraindications for patients have large gland sizes. Those would be patients that may not be ideal for it. But those patients in general are few. So if patients have not significant lower urinary tract symptoms and are able to receive general anesthesia, they're generally a candidate for breakchie therapy in some form. You also asked about patients and radiation safety. Radiation safety is a potential concern of patients. The in permanent seed implantation, patients receive that treatment from inside the body over the course of about 3 months. In general, the radiation safety issues are limited, but we do give patients who do receive permanent seed implantation uh a card just in case they set off radiation detectors at say an airport or other facility. Some men though are hesitant in that they have grandkids and they want to be able to freely interact with them. In HDR breakchie therapy, there is no permanent seat implantation. So there is no radioactivity when the patients go home and there are no radiation safety concerns after discharge. Dr. Tonk, this is such an interesting episode. === FILE: Penn Pregnancy Early Access Center (PEACE) [843nZu7C0b8].en.txt ===

Welcome to the podcast series from the specialists at Pen Medicine. I'm Melanie Cole and today we're highlighting the PEN Pregnancy Early Access Center or the Peace Program and the contraceptive services offered through the peace program. Joining me is Dr. Serita Sonelkar. She's an associate professor of obstetrics and gynecology at the hospital of the University of Pennsylvania. Dr. Dr. Sonkar, thank you so much for joining us today. What is the peace program at Penn Medicine? Give us a little overview of what this program is. >> Hi Melanie, it's so nice to be here today with you and I'm very excited to talk to you about the peace program. So peace is the Penny Early Access Center and it's an integrated family planning and urgent pregnancy care center that bridges a major gap for people who can become pregnant or who are pregnant. For those looking to prevent pregnancy, peace offers timely, efficient appointments for patient- centered contraception counseling and contraception service provision. And for those who are early in pregnancy, Peace provides a range of services including counseling and early ultrasound for people that are experiencing concerning symptoms like bleeding and also pregnancy options counseling and abortion care as well as miscarriage management. >> That's so important. Tell us a little bit about the contraceptive options that you offer because I mean there's so many today. Tell us a little bit about the ones that you prefer or how you work with the patient in shared decisionm to decide on one of the options. It's true there are a lot of different options and it can be kind of confusing for patients to know even where to start when they come to the doctor asking for these methods. So we offer counseling and provision of all forms of female contraception including IUDs, implants, pills, patches, rings and injectables. We also do pre-operative consultations and surgical permanent contraception using laparoscopic bilateral self injectctomy which is removal of the fallopian tubes. And then we'll discuss with patients how to optimize the use of other non-prescription methods like condoms or fertility awareness if that's what they want to use. and even withdrawal depending on what works best for them. >> Well, then how do you decide with patients what method is best for them? How do you help them decide? And I imagine the age and reproductive years and reproductive future are in discussion there. >> That's exactly right. Those are two really important aspects of contraception counseling. The approach is generally a very careful balance of person- centered and evidence-based counseling. We know that each patient has personal and unique values around their reproductive lives. And there's no one overall goal standard method for contraception. So, we use, like you said, a shared decision-making approach. First, we will have a conversation with the patient about what's most important to them. So it might be making sure that their method is safe in the context of other medical conditions or maybe they want to reduce or stop heavy bleeding with their periods. Maybe they want to carefully time their pregnancy around optimization of their medical conditions. Or maybe they just want the most effective or permanent method. So once we have that conversation and understand what they value most, we can then tailor our recommendations to them. basically saying that this is the method or these are the methods that could potentially meet the needs that you have and we use the highest quality and most up-to-date evidence around contraception in order to help them make those decisions. Now, people are not always aware that contraception is not only to prevent pregnancy but also used in some cases for other health concerns that a woman might have including pain management. So, how does your approach to pain management for IUD insertion and removal differ from a routine obstitrician gynecologist? Tell us a little bit about that. >> I think there are two parts to your question. One, I think contraception can be used not specifically for pregnancy prevention, but also for underlying conditions like painful periods or really heavy periods or maybe pain with endometriosis. And so we will help people choose a contraceptive method that might help them manage their pain related to other conditions related to the reproductive system. When it comes to pain management for IUD insertions, many people know that insertion of an IUD is a relatively invasive procedure that can be painful. And we will talk to patients about their pain management options when placing an IUD. And we'll use a trauma-informed approach to all our pelvic exams and procedures. Meaning that we basically address their psychological, their emotional, and their physical needs. And then for the procedure itself, we have a variety of different techniques to reduce pain. I would say the cornerstone of that is a local anesthetic that we inject into the cervix prior to placing the IUD, which has been shown in multiple randomized control trials to reduce pain levels. and the proportion of people who experience severe pain and this is particularly for people who haven't delivered a baby before. But we offer numbing medication into the cervix basically for all of our patients and also offer other oral medications, heating pads and just a calming approach to care. And in addition, we will offer IUD insertions under siation if that is really what's necessary for the patient to achieve the pain management goals that they have. such a comprehensive approach for women. Now, what are they saying about the peace program? What is the patient experience like with your program at pen medicine? >> The number one thing that patients will say to me is that that was way better than I thought it was going to be. And I'm always very happy when I hear that. I also am a little bit saddened by the fact that so many people come in so afraid of the pain that they're going to experience. But I'm glad that we're able to help them through the process and make them feel comfortable. They also really enjoy the fact that we are very kind. We don't rush them through their procedures. We often have somebody who can hold their hand during the procedures if they need that. And many patients when they're done with their IUD insertion are able to leave and go home in a really comfortable state. >> Doctor, thank you so much. Now, I'd like you to speak to referring physicians about patient selection for the program. What patients should providers consider referring to your program? And I'd like you to summarize the key takeaways about the important work that you're doing and communication with those referring physicians. >> I think it's really important to know that any patient in their reproductive years who has a uterus has the potential to become pregnant. And even with medical conditions, patients with disabilities, all of those patients deserve a comprehensive approach to reproductive life planning, which includes pregnancy planning and contraception care if that's something that they want. And so for our program, we're really happy to see any patient who is in their reproductive years and would like information or services related to family planning, whether that's contraception care, early pregnancy evaluation, abortion, miscarriage. We really welcome patients with medical complexity, patients with disabilities and we take all types of insurance including public and private insurance. So I think patients whether they're at risk for pregnancy, want to be pregnant or want to help with pregnancy prevention and they are a person that they can refer to our program. We are happy to see them. I'd also like to add that patients can find us directly by calling 610924989. Option five is peace and that is a number that providers can give to patients if they want to reach the peace program directly. >> Thank you so much doctor for joining us today and telling us about the peace program at Penn Medicine and to refer your patient to Dr. Sonolcar at Penn Medicine. Please call our 247 provider line at 877-937 PEN or you can submit your referral via our secure online referral form by visiting our website at penmed.org/refer your patient. That concludes this episode from the specialists at pen medicine. I'm Melanie Cole.

=== FILE: Penn Running & Endurance Sports Program with Dr. Vasudevan [HS9wYT8EbRI].en.txt ===

Welcome to the podcast series from the specialists at Pen Medicine. I'm Melanie Cole and joining me today is Dr. John Basudan. He's director of the Pen Medicine running and endurance sports program and an associate professor of clinical physical medicine and rehabilitation at Penn Medicine. And he's here to highlight for us the Penn Running and Endurance Sports Program. Dr. Vasuan, it's a pleasure to have you join us today. So tell us about the pen running and endurance sports program. What makes it unique when it comes to treating runners and other endurance athletes? Well, first of all, thank you for having me. It's a pleasure and privilege to be here. What I'm hoping to discuss a little bit today is what the running and endurance sports program at Penn Medicine has to offer that is unique and directed towards athletes in our area or region that can best take care of this certain population of endurance athletes. If you're a runner or any type of athlete, if you're a swimmer, if you're a cyclist, or regardless of your sport, you're going to run into injury at some point. Some of these injuries are ones that are just nagging. Sometimes can stop you in your tracks. There are more than enough qualified physicians in this area that can treat injuries. But what I want to understand better is helping someone achieve a goal. Sometimes people get so focused on treating that knee that hurts that we lose sight of why what we would do if that knee wasn't hurting. So, I put together a group of physicians, physical therapists, and many other different specialists who speak the language of the sport and understand what they're trying to achieve. I love that you use the term speak the language of the sport because that really is true. I'd like you to speak about some of the conditions that the pen running program team evaluate and treat. You mentioned knees, but of course, runners have all sorts of issues. Absolutely. We treat a wide variety of conditions mostly involving joints and tendons. So when it comes to runners obviously hip, knee and ankle joint issues are big and depending on the age that could be something like a meniscus tear or a laboral tear. It could be something as advanced as osteoarthritis at a certain age. When it comes to tendon issues, oftentimes that can involve glutial teninopathy, patellar teninopathy, achilles, and not forgetting that sometimes swimmers and cyclists can also run into injuries as well as runners just in their crossraining involving things like the shoulder joint, rotator cuff, and tendon issues of the elbows like lateral or medial epicondilitis. So those are some of the conditions. But one thing I learned in medical school is that the kneebone is connected to the hipbone is connected to the backbone. So sometimes people come in with one achy joint, but you realize it is the consequence of a movement pattern that we need to improve in order to take care not only that pain, but prevent others from coming. I'm glad you brought up cross trainining because that does help with some of the injuries that we see in the field and especially with such dedicated athletes as runners are. Can you walk us through the process that patients go through when they're evaluated, diagnosed, treated by the pen running program? Tell us a little bit about your program and the multiddisciplinary approach. When you first engage with the pen running and endurance sports program, it's going to feel at first like a typical doctor's office. You're going to come in, you fill out your paperwork, I take your history, examine you, and so on, take a look at any kind of imaging or other diagnostic workup you have or perform some at that time like a simple X-ray. But what then is atypical and maybe additive is depending on what you present with, we may have you run on a treadmill. We may examine your footwear or have a discussion of that things like orthoses that you would use in those footwear or braces that you may have tried and then really delve a little bit further into what is your training program because the treatment that you would a patient would need can vary depending on whether they're trying to do a couch to 5k, whether they're trying to finish their first half marathon or whether they're trying to qualify for the Boston Marathon. So having a a little bit of added time to discuss what their training goals and current program are and then what happens is we'll take all of that and then start coming up with a plan and identify what other disciplines need to be involved. Most commonly that'll be physical therapy. But part of this program is understanding that sometimes it's more than just the mechanical. Sometimes it's dietary and nutrition related. So we have registered dieticians who are focused on sports nutrition in particular. We have sports psychologists. Sometimes half the barrier is not just physically your discomfort but sort of the challenge mentally of kind of wrapping your head around how this injury is getting in the way of things. And sometimes it does require surgical care. Most runners, cyclist, swimmers fortunately don't require that. But sometimes when that it's about identifying when the potential risks of surgery are outweighed by the benefit in the long term for other providers. Doctor, what makes someone a good candidate for the pen running and endurance sports program? The best kind of candidates are fitnessoriented, but it's really about what you want to get accomplished. I love seeing a patient who has a goal in mind. And so I always try to relay back to my referring physicians what the goal is because I think it makes such a big difference. I'll take anything from beginning to the highle elite as long as they have that goal in mind because sometimes it's really just about establishing a pattern of fitness. Sometimes someone's already been there and they just want to enhance their performance to meet that goal. When do you feel it's important that they refer their patients? When is it you'd like them to look into the program and say to their patients, "This is the time." The goal of this program is to learn how we can best standardize assessments between physical therapists and physicians. (upbeat music) - I'm Dr. Arlet, I'm an orthopaedic spine surgeon. - I'm Dr. Ozturk, I'm a neurosurgeon here at Penn Medicine. And today we're going to be talking about adult spinal deformity. When people think about scoliosis, they usually think of younger patients, but in fact, it's extremely common in adults. A lot of these are nonsurgical and they're asymptomatic, but many can progress and become very painful, and they are amenable to surgery. - People older than 70 years of age have a 70% chance to have a 15 degree scoliosis. So I have lots of people around us who have scoliosis and it's very common in the adult population. - If it progresses oftentimes past a curvature of 30 degrees, 40 degrees, it can be very painful, leading to a curve of the spine and sometimes with a patient listing towards one side. There can also be deformities in the sagittal plane which Dr. Arlet can tell us about. - Yes, we see a number of patients who have what we call a flat back, that means they are not able to stand up straight and they stand up stooped forward. They cannot stand up straight and this is very painful, very demanding on the back. We have another category of patient we see quite often, is a patient who had multiple spine surgeries done elsewhere, and whether the surgery didn't address the initial problem or whether the surgery got a complication or whether it's a natural history of the aging process, they need to address this new problem, so to relieve that pain and get them straighter with a better balance. As the spine gets older, the discs lose some of their height, they may collapse to one side. So causing asymmetry either to the side or forward, then you get a nerve impingement. The nerve gets pinched to some extent creating spinal stenosis. So patients come with a complex situation where you have a spinal stenosis and curvature of the spine. - It's the price we pay for being upright after 70 years, people are living longer and longer. But as Dr. Arlet mentioned, it tends to be an asymmetric degeneration of the adult spine, which can lead to a curvature of the spine either to the side or forward. All of which can be very painful. We have special x-ray machines here with our EOS machine, which takes a picture of the entire skeleton of the human body and it really lets us appreciate the alignment. We frequently get both CAT scans, MRIs, electromyography, which is a clinical test that our neurologists help us perform and most importantly, the clinical history and the physical exam. We have to put all these together to make sure that we're operating on a correct diagnosis. - The one thing that patients should know about this EOS machine is that the amount of radiation that's delivered with this machine is one fifth. So that means the people who come to Penn to get these x-rays have 80% less radiation than conventional x-rays done elsewhere. - I think probably one of our biggest assets is the experience of the entire hospital and the team, from our anesthesiologists to our electrophysiologists, to our surgeons, to the nursing care, to the ICU care. I think we're all used to dealing with this and that's probably our biggest asset. In the operating room, we have the ability to monitor the function of the patient's nerves. So if we're doing anything to irritate the nerves of the spinal cord, we have immediate feedback. We have intraoperative CAT scanners, x-rays, a lot of safety mechanisms that are nice to have in place to make these operations safer. - You should see the OR at Pennsylvania Hospital where we have a huge number of spinal surgeries that are done every year, we're doing more than 2000 spine surgeries every year. And so whether it's the scrub tech who is helping us out, the spine technologist who is helping us out, everybody knows how we work, everybody knows what their role is and this makes the surgery very successful, it goes faster. Many places we hear about surgery that lasts 12 hours, when we know we do them in six, seven hours here. - I think this is the sort of surgery that you probably would be ill-advised to have it in a place that does a few a year. We do at least several a week. - And the important thing is that patient expectations are real and we meet the expectations of the patient when we talk to them so they can be happy when we've done the treatment or we operate on them. - This is one of the rare conditions that I think that we can actually call it a cure if done properly and if the spine is properly realigned, and it's extremely gratifying to see these patients back in my clinic, oftentimes they give you a big warm hug and it's very satisfying.
