=== FILE: Penn Transplant Institute： Living Donor Kidney Transplant Education [k9gGAERZt0s].en.txt ===

Welcome to the Penn Center for Living Donations education session. Today we will be reviewing the process for living kidney donation. Before we get started, I'd like to take a moment to recognize your inspiring altruism and generosity in considering being evaluated as a living kidney donor. It is our hope that this information will assist you in making a well-informed decision about living kidney donation. The purpose of this video is to review all aspects of living kidney donation. Together, we will be covering all of the information you see here. We will review general information about your kidneys, an overview of living donation, including alternatives for donors and recipients, and confidentiality associated with the process. We will review our multiddisciplinary team including roles and responsibilities, the donor process including screening, referral evaluation and donor selection. We will discuss paired kidney exchange and the voucher program. We will review preparation for surgery, the donor surgery itself, potential risks and complications as well as your expected hospital stay and followup with our team. And finally, you will hear about short-term and long-term living donor outcomes, financial considerations, and resources and support for individuals like yourself going through a living kidney donor evaluation. We encourage you to take notes regarding any questions that may arise during the presentation so that you can review them with your living donor coordinator. Let's start with some general information. We will now talk about your kidneys. You have two kidneys located in the middle part of your back on the right and left side of your spine. They are behind the majority of your abdominal organs. The kidneys play an important role in our bodies. They remove waste, toxins, and extra fluids. The kidneys balance electrolytes. They control blood pressure through adjustment of fluids, electrolytes, and release of hormones. The kidneys help support red blood cell production and overall keep you healthy. They make urine and urine is the byproduct of removing toxins and managing the balance of electrolytes. You only need one kidney to live a healthy and fulfilling life. One can safely be donated while the other remains in place. During the evaluation process, we review your kidney function and overall health to ensure that your health will not be compromised with one kidney. Things you should know. Patients with endstage kidney disease have the option of pursuing transplant or using kidney replacement therapy, which is also known as dialysis. For a kidney transplant, the kidney can come from either a deceased donor or a living donor. Receiving a kidney from a living donor has many advantages over one from a deceased donor. Living kidney donor recipients have better outcomes. A living donor kidney typically starts working immediately, whereas 30 to 50% of deceased donor kidneys take up to two weeks to start working. This means that a living donor transplant recipient is less likely to need dialysis shortly after surgery. In addition to working immediately, living donor kidneys last longer. Recipients of a living donor kidney have shorter hospital stays and even fewer complications. Wait times for deceased donor kidneys are long. There is little or no weight for an organ from a living kidney donor, whereas the weight for a deceased donor kidney is 5 years on average. Organ allocation regulations are changing and the wait time for a deceased donor organ offer could be longer in the future. The process of finding a kidney donor can be challenging for recipients. Individuals are asked to advocate for themselves to identify a living kidney donor and those in need of a kidney transplant can talk with their transplant team about how to get started. Living donation is a voluntary act and you as the donor have the option to change your mind up until the point of general anesthesia. We offer you a medical alibi if needed. In other words, you can choose to opt out of the process without anyone outside of the living donor team being notified. Recipients have other options for kidney replacement therapy, including dialysis, disease donor transplant, listing at multiple centers, or exploration of alternative living donor options, confidentiality, and disclaimers. As a potential kidney donor, you have several rights. As we already discussed, you have the right to opt out of this process at any time. Additionally, your health information is secure and separate from the recipient's record. Only the necessary information is shared with your recipient's team. Similarly, the recipient health information is also confidential and protected under privacy laws. All communication is strictly confidential. Recipients may be informed that there is a donor in evaluation, that a donor has been approved, or that there are no potential living donors to consider. You, as a potential donor, are able to share as much or as little information with your recipient as you like. It is a federal crime to sell or purchase human organs. You as the donor cannot receive anything of valuable consideration in exchange for donation, including monetary gifts. Although rare, donation could have an impact on obtaining health, life, or disability insurance in the future. We review these impacts with you during your individual evaluation. It is not okay to be coerced into donating a kidney. If you feel any pressure in donating, please notify the donor team immediately. And finally, this presentation will highlight important information so you can provide informed consent regarding potential kidney donation. Now we will review the living donor team. As a potential living donor, you will meet many members of the multiddisciplinary team during the evaluation process. You, as the donor, are the most important member of this team. The independent living donor advocate or ILDA is a specialized social worker who works with the team. We will review the roles of the shortly. Your living donor nurse coordinator is your main point of contact throughout your donor evaluation. You will interact with many of the health care professionals listed here, including your donor surgeon, kidney specialist or nefologist, advanced practice provider or a different type of social worker who sits apart from the ILDA. You may also interact with a financial coordinator as well as our pharmacist who will review your current medications. You may be asked to meet with a dietitian, psychiatrist, or other specialists as part of the evaluation as well. This is at the discretion of the donor team. We will now review each member of the team's role and responsibilities in more detail. Roles and responsibilities of the independent living donor advocate. As mentioned, the independent living donor advocate or ILDA is a specialized type of social worker that meets with you during the evaluation. All transplant centers in the United States are required to provide an ILA team for all potential donors. This works independently but collaboratively with the donor team. As you know, living organ donation is completely voluntary. The role of the is to protect the donor's health and safety. The sole job of the is to protect and promote the interests of the donor and support the donor through the entire process. Thea assists you in obtaining, educating, and understanding all relevant information. They will review the consent process, the evaluation process, surgical procedure, medical and psychosocial risks, financial risks, and the importance of and commitment to post-donation followup. The ILA will respect the donor's decision and ensure that the decision is informed, free from pressure, and without financial compensation. The next person from our team that you've interacted with is your living donor nurse coordinator. Our living donor coordinators are your main point of contact with the living donor team. The living donor nurse coordinator screens inquiries, escalates and communicates information to the team, facilitates the evaluation process, educates donors and families in all phases of care. They help prepare the donor for surgery, coordinates progression of the case with the recipient team, acts as a clinical resource to the donor, and answers questions and facilitates post-donation care. Other members of the living donor team are listed here. The living donor surgeon, kidney specialist, and a all work together. They review your individual risks for kidney donation and set expectations for the evaluation, surgery, and post-operative period. They discuss the risks of living donor surgery and will determine if you need individualized testing or require consultation with other specialists. The social worker reviews your financial and social support, provides information on donor assistance programs, and assesses psychosocial issues related to donation. A psychiatrist that works exclusively with the living donor team assesses your mental health history and coping mechanisms to ensure that it is not only physically appropriate but emotionally and psychosoccially appropriate for you to donate. Our dietician assesses if your weight is healthy for surgery and whether you need to make any changes in the short or long term to maintain healthy habits. The pharmacist reviews your medications. They may recommend you discontinue some medications before surgery. And finally, the financial coordinator works to prevent charges associated with living donation from being build to the donor. The donor's evaluation process is covered under the recipient's health insurance and the living donor should not incur any costs related to evaluation or donation. We are now going to talk a little more about the donation process. The living organ donation process is made up of many steps. This begins with the screening of your online referral form followed by education, informed consent, and the medical, surgical, and psychological evaluation. We then move on to the donor selection and approval phase. If you are approved, we begin preparing for surgery by scheduling your pre-operative visits and the surgery itself. Following surgery, we have the post-operative recovery in the hospital as well as the care following hospital discharge. Screening criteria. In order to donate a kidney, you need to be in very good physical and mental health. Your body mass index or BMI must be less than 35. You must be between the ages of 18 and 70 years old. Slightly older candidates are considered on a case-byase basis. Non-directed donors or donors without an identified recipient must be at least 21 years of age. We do require you to have a primary care doctor as well as health insurance. You may request a copy of our donor or recipient selection criteria by contacting your coordinator directly. The evaluation phase can take a minimum of four to six weeks. This includes an assessment by the ILDA as well as a thorough medical and surgical evaluation. You will complete a psychosocial evaluation in which you will meet with our social worker and you may even be asked to meet with our psychiatrist. You will also complete all diagnostic and lab testing. We require donor candidates to be up todate on all age appropriate cancer screenings such as mammogram, papsmear, and colonoscopies. These routine tests should be completed through your primary care provider. Please bring a copy of your results to our team for review. Some candidates will be asked to meet with other specialists, which may include cardiology, infectious disease, or hematology. Some parts of this evaluation or tests may need to be repeated after 6 months have lapsed to ensure you remain eligible to donate. There are risks to donor evaluation. During the evaluation, you will have a CT scan which requires IV contrast. It is possible there could be an allergic reaction to the contrast agent used during the CT scan. Due to the testing that is required, we may discover reportable infections or serious medical conditions that can prevent donation and would require follow-up with your primary care doctor. We may discover previously unknown or adverse genetic findings. These findings may require additional testing at your own expense. All of our decisions are focused on the safety of the donor. Long-term medical implications of organ donation have not been fully identified. There are potential risks to the kidney donor surgery and this will be discussed further with you during your evaluation. Donor selection and approval. At each point in the evaluation process, your results will be made available to you. The multiddisciplinary team meets regularly to review the safety for each patient to donate. The multi-disiplinary committee's decision will be shared with you directly. You may be declined, approved, or the team may recommend additional testing. If you are approved, you will have time to reflect on your decision. In the event you decide to opt out of this process, your decision will be kept completely confidential. If you choose to proceed, the recipient team will be notified that a donor has been approved. After you are approved, the team reviews your matching and suitability for direct donation. Paired kidney exchange is a solution for incompatible pairs. The team may recommend you donate through the paired kidney exchange program if you are incompatible by age, blood type, matching, kidney size, or even anatomy. In this program, your kidney would be transplanted into an anonymous recipient and your intended recipient who needs the kidney would receive a living donor kidney from an anonymous donor. Even if you are compatible with your recipient, the donor may elect to donate through the paired exchange. We refer to this as compatible paired donation. This allows the donor to maximize their gift by helping more than one recipient get transplanted. Here at Penn, we participate in paired exchange through the national kidney registry. There are many benefits of using the paired kidney exchange program. Better match longerlasting. Donating through paired exchange allows the recipient to get a better match kidney, which means that it may last longer. We also improve transplant outcomes. Parrot exchange and living donation both allow the transplant to occur before the recipient needs dialysis. Research shows that less time on dialysis is better for the transplanted kidney and for patients overall. This program also removes uncertainty and allows people to schedule conveniently using PAR exchange. The surgery can be scheduled at the optimal time for both the donor and the recipient. Pen medicine participates in the NKR's paired kidney exchange program. The NKR's voucher program or the advanced donation program allows a living kidney donor to choose the most convenient time frame for their donation surgery regardless of when the recipient is ready for transplant. There are a variety of re reasons that donor and recipient pairs utilize the voucher program. Advanced donation allows the donor and recipient to avoid recovering at the same time. Donors may also wish to schedule their surgery within a specific time frame due to work life commitments. This program is often used when the donor is ready for surgery, but the recipient is not yet ready for transplant. The voucher program is also utilized by nondirected donors. Non-directed donors wish to help others in need but have not yet identified a specific recipient. Non-directed donors donate a kidney to an anonymous recipient within the NKR. In return, they receive a family voucher, which looks out for the family's potential future kidney transplant needs. On the family voucher, the donor identifies five family members or friends that if they were ever in need of a kidney transplant, the first person in need would receive a living donor kidney transplant through the registry. Your living donor coordinator can provide you with additional information on the advanced donation and voucher programs. Now we will take some time to discuss the donor surgery. Preparing for surgery. A date for surgery will be identified that is suitable for the donor, recipient, and transplant team. Special circumstances exist for distance donors and international donors. If you live more than 3 hours from our center, we may require you to stay locally for a period of time after surgery. Pre-operative visit. There is no special diet necessary to prepare you for surgery. We encourage you to make healthy food choices. Some patients are asked to maintain or continue to lose weight. You should avoid dietary supplements for 1 to two weeks before surgery. We recommend that all donors abstain from alcohol for 4 weeks before and 4 weeks after surgery. The pre-operative appointment is typically scheduled on a Monday approximately 1 to two weeks prior to surgery. This visit is 3 to four hours long. During this time, you will have your pre-operative labs drawn. You will meet with team members, including a nurse coordinator, advanced practice provider, and donor surgeon. You will review expectations for recovery and sign the surgical consents. The day of surgery, you will arrive very early on the morning of surgery at the hospital of the University of Pennsylvania Pavilion, Clifton Center. You will meet with an anesthesiologist who explains the risks of general anesthesia. You will be sedated for approximately 4 hours. Monitoring and assisted devices will be placed, including a breathing tube for the ventilator, a foley catheter in your bladder to drain urine, and external monitoring sensors. Remember that your surgical team is focused on your safety. If at any point the team believes you are at risk of significant complications or death, the surgery will be stopped. You as a donor are able to change your mind up until you are sedated. What to expect during surgery. You will be having an efrectomy in which one of your kidneys will be removed. The surgeon will discuss which kidney will be removed as well as the incisions when you meet with them. The majority of our surgeries are done laparoscopically or robotically which uses small incisions. This requires two to five small incisions that are less than a half an inch in length. The camera and surgical instruments are inserted into these small incisions. The kidney is removed through a larger incision. Our surgeons typically place the main incision in incision either at your pant line or near your belly button. Absorbable sutures are used at all incisions and healing takes at least 4 to 6 weeks. There will be discomfort during the recovery, but we will work hard to ensure your pain is manageable. In very rare circumstances, blood transfusion may be needed during or after the surgery. After surgery, you will wake up in the post anesthesia care unit or PACU. You will stay here for close monitoring of your vital signs while you continue to wake up from anesthesia. You will then be transferred to the abdominal transplant floor at the HUP Pavilion Clifton Center. Donors are typically discharged after staying one or two nights in the hospital. We will be reviewing the milestones for discharge shortly. The recovery period at home is typically 4 to 6 weeks. Most donors are able to return to usual activities after 4 weeks. However, you will still have restrictions on activities and lifting. Donors are permitted to return to more demanding activities and heavy lifting after 3 months. The hospital stay and going home. Following surgery, your goals are to get out of bed early and ambulate frequently. Once you are permitted to walk in the halls, you should do this a few times per day. Deep breathing. We want you to keep breathing deeply to keep your lungs open. Pain management. We will ensure your pain is manageable. Your pain should be at a level that allows you to take deep breaths and walk around. Advancing diet. Your diet will be advanced to a regular diet. Donors are discharged when they are able to stay hydrated and tolerate food. Their pain is managed appropriately and they are able to walk in the halls without assistance. Donors are discharged from the hospital with medications to treat pain and constipation. As you learned earlier, kidney donor surgery is minimally invasive and has a low rate of complications, but this is still a surgery and all surgeries carry potential risks. I'm going to take the next few moments to review the risks related to kidney donation. There are medical risks related to surgery, which we have categorized as mild, moderate, and major. There are also potential mental health and financial risks. Minor medical risks require little or no treatment and include an infection at your wound or IV site, urinary tract infection, pneumonia, or an increase in blood pressure. Moderate risks require a procedure to treat the donor and these include blood clot, bleeding, decrease in kidney function, hernia, pain or numbness at the surgical site, discomfort with stretching or moving, bowel obstruction, and urinary retention. Major life-threatening risks include collapsed lung, death, kidney failure requiring dialysis, and complications related to future pregnancies. Mental health risks include new or increased anxiety regarding dependence on others, generalized anxiety, feelings of guilt or sadness, post-traumatic stress disorder, and depression. Financial risks include future health problems related to donation that might not be covered by your insurance. There is a possibility that you may be denied medical insurance, disability benefits, or even life insurance in the future. We will now review post-donation care, post- discharge precautions and restrictions. It is important that you follow these restrictions after surgery. Activity and lifestyle adjustments. Light activity like walking is encouraged early on, but heavy lifting and strenuous exercise should be avoided for several weeks. Donors should not lift, push, or pull more than 10 lbs for the first 6 weeks following surgery. This is crucial to avoid hernia and injury. You should not drive for the first two weeks at a minimum. Returning to work depends on pain control, energy levels, and lifting requirements. Most donors resume normal routines within four to six weeks. If your job requires you to lift more than 50 pounds, you will require a full 3 months off for recovery. We will discuss your restrictions in more detail at your follow-up clinic visit. Medication and self-care. Donors should avoid certain medications like non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or NSAIDs. This class includes medications like ibuprofen, Motrin and neproxin. Donors should also avoid using herbal supplements. Pain will be managed with the prescribed medications. Hydration and nutrition support healing during this time. Monitoring for health changes. Any serious health issue like infection or cancer must be reported to our center as they may affect the recipient. The transplant team will coordinate care and report if needed. Although rare, it is possible that you may not return to your pre-donation lifestyle. You may experience body image issues, guilt, anxiety, or depression. If you feel you are becoming depressed or chronically anxious, please get help and talk to your healthcare provider. Many donors find it helpful to speak with friends, family, and other donors during this time. Post-surgical followup. We will follow you for the first two years after surgery. Here you can see an outline of the required followup after donation. Regular followup is important for your overall health as well as the health of your remaining kidney. 3 weeks after surgery, you will meet with your surgical team for an in-person clinic visit and complete lab testing. At this visit, we will assess your progress, review your activity restrictions, and answer any questions you might have. Six months after surgery, you will see our nephrology team. Visits can occur via telea medicine or in-person visits in Philadelphia. Blood and urine tests are required and should be completed one week before the visit. At the one-year and two-year anniversaries, you will speak with our team to review your blood pressure, current health status, and recent lab work. Our team may require a tele medicine or in-person nefrology visit at this time. After donation, it is important to stay up to date with your annual physicals with your primary care provider. All follow-up kidney labs will be ordered by and reviewed by our team for the first two years after surgery. Thereafter, you will continue to have your regular annual follow-up with your primary care doctor or local nefologist. Reportable conditions after donation. There are some medical conditions that if they develop must be reported to the transplant center as they may affect the health of the recipient. Examples include any infectious disease or cancer discovered in the first two years. If one of these conditions occurs, we are required to notify certain organizations. We may be required to notify the recipient of your kidney, local, state, or federal public health authorities as this is required by law, the recipient transplant center, and a national donor database, the OPT, improving safety portal. If your doctor suspects that a health issue is related to donation, please notify your living donor coordinator as soon as possible. Our living donor team will coordinate a clinical evaluation here at Penn Transplant Institute. We will now review donor resources and support. financial information and billing. The recipient's insurance typically covers your medical expenses, but some insurance carriers have special requirements to cover living donors as part of the recipient insurance. While our goal is to minimize any expenses, there may be expenses to you. Financial responsibilities associated with living donation, including post-donation expenses, may not be covered by insurance. Unfortunately, insurance does not cover expenses related to travel or lost wages, but you may be eligible for financial support. There are two different programs that offer support for things such as lost wages, travel costs, or even dependent care. The National Living Donor Assistance Center, or NLDAC, commonly known as NADAC, is available to all donors. The National Kidney Registry's donor shield program is available to all patients that donate here at Penn. Please discuss your interest in these programs when you meet with our social worker. They will be able to answer additional questions and assist you with the process. The National Kidney Registry offers benefits to living donors through their donor shield program. All pen living donors are eligible. The benefits of this program include lost wage reimbursement, donation related travel costs, lodging, meals, dependent care, and pet care. Additional protection in the event you develop a complication, legal support to assist with life insurance discrimination or unlawful employment termination. In the unlikely event that you would need a transplant, the National Kidney Registry prioritizes you to receive a living donor kidney from their registry. For additional information and the most up-to-date information, you can visit donorshield.com/kidney or scan the QR code that you see here. Outcome data for living donors and recipients. Outcome data for both national and center specific outcomes is available for your review through the scientific registry of transplant recipients or srtt.org. There are no national or centers specific outcomes for living donors calculated by the SRTR. We encourage you to review the data so you can be aware of the national results as well as Penn's recipient outcomes. Our team is available to you to discuss donor and recipient outcomes here at Penn Transplant Institute. Please contact us directly with any questions. The Clyde Barker Transplant House is a guest house for transplant patients and caregivers who reside at least 25 miles from the hospital of the University of Pennsylvania. Our patients often utilize a transplant house for outpatient appointments or even after discharge from the hospital. The Clyde Barker transplant house offers many amenities that you see listed here. The cost of staying at the transplant house is deeply discounted. Please call the number you see here for reservation or additional information. Our team is available to you 24 hours a day, 7 days per week, and 365 days per year. Our team includes a surgeon, physician, transplant nurse coordinator, and advanced practice providers. We receive organ offers, recover donor organs, perform the transplant surgeries, and address urgent clinical needs for all of our patients. You will be notified within 7 to 10 business days if there is a change in our ability to provide this coverage. In the event of a local or regional emergency that impacts our ability to provide transplant care, we will use available resources to notify you and identify a local or regional center to help transfer your care. There are multiple regulatory bodies involved in kidney donation and transplantation. The United Network for Organ Sharing or UNOS is the federal agency that oversees organ donation and transplant. UNOS keeps the national patient waiting list for organ transplants. If you have a question or would like to file a grievance, you should contact Penn Transplant Institute Administration or UNOS directly. The scientific registry of transplant recipients or SRTR publishes public national and trans transplant center recipient outcome data. Data is used to compare transplant center outcomes. Lastly, we have the center for Medicare services or CMS. Penn transplant institute has met all requirements by CMS. We will notify you if our CMS or Medicare status changes in the future. If you have any further questions about these regulatory requirements, please contact your transplant coordinator. This concludes our education session today. My name is Maria, and I'm an LPN with Penn Medicine Home Health Lancaster. I visit patients in their home when they get discharged from the hospital, or if they have any cares that need to be met at their home. I chose home care over another setting because you feel like you're not just in one place, you don't feel like you’re in four walls. Sometimes I go to the country and that just relaxes me. You're not always back-to-back doing the same things. I usually start my day around 8, 8:30. While my kids are getting ready for school, I'm prepping my work. Once I'm done with my work, I clock out, I take my daughter to school. Once I get to my first patient, I clock back in and that's when I start my day. - Hey, Maria. - Hello, how are you? - Good, come on in, it's so nice out. - Yes it is, you ready? - I'm ready, come on in. Once I get to a patient's home, I get my laptop. I have all the information on my computer, and as I'm doing my assessment, I'm charting everything, so you have everything in your hands. - And you're still using the wheelchair to get around? - Yes, and my scooter. Here at Penn, you feel like you're supported with your managers, whether it's within the work, or your life at home. If you need help, they’re always there to support you and guide you along. We are trusted that we're doing what we need to do out in the community to help patients. I trust that they have my back. It makes me feel good to be able to help people that are not able to go out, because I know that they're getting the care they need. By my eyes, by pictures, by assessments. You actually get to be able to just focus on that person and focus on their needs. I would like to take advantage of Penn Medicine tuition reimbursement because I want to get my RN completed. That's part of my goal within the next five years, maybe less. I am actually in the middle of getting my certification for my wound care, and that's one of my favorite things to do.  I love doing wound care. - In the meantime, make sure that you elevate as much as you can, and take care of yourself and we’ll see you Friday. - Alright, thank you. - I drive my own vehicle to work, and it also helps now that Penn Medicine gives us a reimbursement for our mileage, which helps me offset anything that I need to do for my vehicle, any gas that I spend. I love what I do. I love being able to help the community. I am bilingual, so I love being able to help those Spanish-speaking patients who don't understand English, but when they see that it's a Spanish-speaking nurse, it makes everything so much better for them. When people hear Penn Medicine, it’s always something good.

(gentle music) - A memory cafe is a safe space for socialization for folks with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, or really any kind of cognitive impairment to get out of the house, to connect with other people who are experiencing similar symptoms without the fear of judgment or stigma, but also just kind of forget, maybe, about their diagnosis and what they're going through and feel sort of a little bit more like their old selves. - It cheers me up. Look, with one thing and another, I'm not always as cheerful as I might be. At these things, I do feel happier. I like the comedy, I like the music, I like the conversation. (laughing) - [Alison] Sometimes, unfortunately, the friends and family who they've met don't know how to cope with this situation, don't know how to talk to someone with cognitive impairment, don't know how to engage them, and so they tend to drop away, I think, not because they care, but because they're uncomfortable or scared and don't know what to do. - Well, it's pretty much you're isolated, you know? You're either in your house or, you know, like I said, there's really not that many places you can go. It's been an enjoyable way out of the life that we live. We're married 40 years, and she took care of me. You know what I mean. - A lot of our patients and their caregivers end up staying at home a lot more and sort of self-isolating, but then here we are in the office saying go get social interaction, that's gonna help slow down the progression of your disease and increase your quality of life. But then, how do they do that? (singing in foreign language) So, it originally started, we had a social work intern, Genevieve Geller, who interned with me about four years ago. And so, she had been reading about memory cafes in the Netherlands, and brought it to our supervisor, now our executive director, Felicia Greenfield, who greenlit it, and basically said, if you can find a space, because we really wanna have these in a non-medicalized space. We didn't want to have it at the hospital, we want it to be sort of free of the feelings that you get when you go to the doctor's office and the anxiety of that. And Christchurch Neighbor House, where we are right now, was able to donate the space to us for our first two years, I believe. And so, for about a year, it was pretty much just donation-based. We didn't have performers the way that we do now. It was really just two hours one Friday morning a month to come together and sit and have casual conversation and coffee. - [Mark] It's a great safe place. You could take your husband, your mother, your father, no matter who has it, they're there and they're amongst other people who have that same disease, and for yourself, it's that you're back in the community. - Usually they have this caregiver, care-recipient connection, but if just for five, 10 minutes they were able to regain that spousal connection doing something that they love, enjoying music, enjoying dancing together. And so, that's what I really like is seeing people kind of forget the difficult emotional reality of sometimes their very acute suffering, and being able to just sort of escape for an hour or two in a safe space. - Some people are here because they have cognitive impairment, and other people are caregivers, and both types of groups of people are terrific to meet and share the experience, so it was great. I love it.

He's the chief in the division of thoracic surgery and an associate professor of surgery at the hospital of the University of Pennsylvania. Welcome gentlemen. I'm so glad to have you with us today. Dr. Kaharuk, I'd like to start with you. Tell us a little bit about esophageal cancer and what are some of the specific risk factors that other providers should be looking to? Yes. In the current era, the vast majority of esophageal cancers are in patients who have uh reflux and oftentimes they are what are called adnocarcinomomas. These occur in people who are overweight, people that experience daily reflux, people that have been treated for reflux in the past. There's also some association between esophageal cancers and exposures and lifestyles that include cigarette smoking and alcohol intake. So I think as a primary care provider, the most important thing to think about is screening those patients who have recurrent reflux over a long period of time. So along those lines, Dr. Dr. Kahartuk, where do you stand as to implementing screening programs for esophageal cancer in the United States? The incidence or number of people with esophageal cancer is growing quickly, but many countries in Asia actually have screening programs both for esophageal and gastric cancer. So at the current time, we have a low threshold for doing endoscopy on patients who have symptoms, but there is no screening recommendation. Yeah, just to follow up on that, you know, if you were to take every single patient of the demographic of patients we see who have reflux or gird, you would be, you know, doing endoscopies on thousands of patients. So, you know, we've not been able yet to bring it down into a system where you may have patients with symptoms for a certain amount of time or the severity before you'd actually scope everybody. You know, at this point in time, we don't have the criteria filled for screening. Dr. Williams, as there are several new advances in surgical treatment, minimally invasive treatments, share some of the latest treatment options that Penn Medicine offers. Tell us about your program and the physician services. What we have in place here is a multid-disciplinary clinic where we we see patients jointly with surgery, with radiation oncology, and with medical oncology. Dr. and I are a thoracic surgeon and a gastrointestinal surgeon respectively and we see patients as a team. The patients come to us either before or after they have had pre-operative chemo radiation therapy. Each person sees the patient. We talk to them individually and also as a team to explain the surgery that we're going to do. What we try to do is to do the majority of the cases in a minimally invasive fashion meaning small incisions in the abdominal portion of the operation and typically we do a trans hiatal esophagectomy which means an abdominal portion of the operation and a small incision in the left side of the neck and the advantage and the beauty of what we do is that we do it as a team. Dr. Kaharuk, as some of the after effects of this type of cancer treatment can affect the daily lives of patients and due to the sensitivity and intricate nature of this cancer, are there some technical considerations you'd like other providers to know about? Sure. I think that there are a couple things that we really need to set out and be very forthright with our patients and their families both for nourishment and pleasure. And part of our goal is to try to restore both of those functions as best as possible. Obviously, the nourishment part of it is critical. And if you don't address the nourishment part early on, you don't have a good outcome. But there is a lot to the social benefits of eating together, of going out. It's a very social undertaking and so we try to restore eating function as close as possible. That's one of the reasons of the four or five different operations we can perform for esophageal cancer. The operation that Dr. Williams spoke about where we put the connection up in the neck uh we like the best. We think that probably gives you the best functional outcome. The straighter, more narrower tubes that are higher up in the body tend to empty better. patients have a better sense of fulfillment with eating and they're still able to maintain their nourishment and meet their requirements to maintain their weight and so that's very important. Dr. Kaharuk, how have your outcomes been? Our outcomes generally are very good. We're a center that's easily doing 40 of these operations a year and because these operations are complex and often times cross multiple body cavities, they're fraught with all kinds of potential complications. But if you have a team that is very experienced, you can smooth out the roller coaster of complications that people often times have in the immediate post-operative period. And then you also have long-term outcome. And what we know about esophageal cancer overall, when you look at the statistics, it is potentially a very deadly cancer that most people don't survive. That being said, if you select patients correctly and you get them the right therapy, you can really start to get appreciable long-term survival rates in patients across several stages, not just early stages, but also patients who are treated with multimodality therapy. And that means they have pre-operative chemo and radiation therapy with nutritional support followed by surgery and then go on for a good long-term cancer outcome. So I think to specifically answer your question, both our short and long-term outcomes are very good. Dr. Kaharuk, if you were to look forward to the next 10 years in the field, what do you feel will be some of the most important areas of research? I think the most exciting thing from my perspective has to do with some of the molecular and genetic profiling of the tumors. There are several tumors that we now find across different body parts that express molecular targets that we can take advantage of. The kind of most recent one in esophageal cancer has been something called herd to new. For listeners who know a little bit about breast cancer, that is something that all breast cancers are tested for. And if you express that on your breast cancer, there is a drug called hercepin which you can give which will improve the outcome. And it's fascinating that just in the last several years, we figured out that a percentage of esophageal cancers do express that and there are some ongoing clinical trials to determine how that drug should be introduced into the overall care pattern. My suspicion is as we test more tumors and get more information, we'll probably see a lot of this crossover and we may see that some of those molecular treatments really change the overall outcome, especially in later stage disease, but they'll probably be incorporated into earlier stage disease as well. And you know, if I could just add to that also, hopefully in the future in relation to esophageal cancer is something called a liquid diagnosis. In other words, you could potentially take a blood test from a a patient, you know, rather than a screening with an endoscopy and lead to an early diagnosis and therefore a higher likelihood of cure. In the advanced stage lung cancer, checking peripheral blood for circulating DNA is standard. As things mature, as the science matures, some of these techniques will be able to be applied to other cancers and in our case hopefully esophageal cancer. So interesting. Absolutely fascinating. What an exciting time to be in this field. === FILE: Penn’s New Chair of Neurosurgery Discusses Neurotechnology [O0zwWNBiUAs].en.txt ===

Welcome to the podcast series from the specialists at Pen Medicine. I'm Melanie Cole and today we're meeting PEN Medicine's new chair of neurosurgery and vice president of clinical integration and innovation, Dr. Daniel Yosher. He's here to discuss his research. Dr. Yosher, it's such a pleasure to have you join us today. You've recently taken part in the development of a neurochnology that's being called the bionic eye. explain a little bit about what this technology is, where we are in its development, and you've said you hope to see the restoration of functional eyesight to the blind in your lifetime. Yes, this has been a tantalizing prospect to neuroscientists and engineers for for quite a long time. And the idea is very simple. Think of a roadblock going around a roadblock. In patients with acquired blindness, almost always it's the eyes, the optic nerves, the early part of the visual processing system that's irreversibly damaged. So visual information can't get from the eyes to the brain because usually the eyes themselves are are damaged or broken. What a visual cortical prosthetic aims to do is take visual information from the outside world and bypass the irreversibly damaged eyes or optic nerves and put that information directly into the visual part of the brain. So the idea is that technology will take images from the outside world, digitize them with a camera and convert that image captured from the outside world into a series of electrical pulses that are used to activate the circuits in the brain that normally allow us to see by getting information directly from the retina and optic nerve. Instead, we bypass the broken retina and optic nerve and deliver the information directly to the brain. That is the concept. That is amazing. Now, is there any reason these implants can't be used in children with inherited blindness or is there something to prevent this? Where do you see it going? That's an excellent question. The way we envision the technology right now, in order for it to work, the visual part of the brain has to be developed. And that development of the visual part of the brain known as the visual cortex, which is mostly located in the back part of the head, those circuits are not developed without the experience of visual inputs that occur during infancy and childhood. So if someone is born with congenital blindness, that part of the brain is not developed and there's no target for us to deliver the visual information. So the technology we're working on will only help patients with acquired blindness. They have to have had some visual function during their lives. It can be early in their lives. They can be blind for many many years but they have to have the latent ability in their visual brain to process visual information. So that would apply to patients who are blind as a result of trauma for example or retinal disorders like retinitis pigmentotosa. Anything that damages the eyes permanently in patients who at one point in their life were able to see relatively normally. those conditions would be appropriate for visual restoration with a visual cortical prosthetic. Doctor, where did the concept for this technology come from? Working in this area for over a decade, what we have largely done in the past is work with patients who are undergoing monitoring for medically intractable epilepsy. These are patients who have epilepsy that can't be controlled with drugs. And these monitoring procedures and surgeries contribute to a better understanding of the visual cortex. What we found and we recently published on this in the journal cell just a couple of months ago in May. I'm very interested in the merger of technology and neurosurgery to improve patient outcomes. And in my practice over the past 20 years, the way I do puritary surgery has changed enormously. And now we do all those surgeries entirely through the nose using endoscopic cameras and special instruments designed for endoscopy. So we do what we call minimally invasive approaches to all these tumors including some very large and challenging tumors. And the great thing about this technology is how much it helps patients. Giving the gift of vision back to patients who are in danger of losing it forever. really uh one of the most gratifying things you can do as a doctor. Dr. Yosher, as we wrap up, as the new chair of neurosurgery and vice president of clinical integration and innovation, what's your vision for the department, what would you like other providers to take away from this episode and what you're planning to do there at Pen Medicine? My vision is to have our department be highly subsp specialcialized with a series of doctors in neurosurgery that are experts in very specific areas in neurosurgery and focused on those very specific areas and that those doctors are not only superb experts in technical neurosurgery within their subsp specialty but they're also harnessing the great science and engineering that we have at Penn to advance the field. So we don't want to just practice medicine at the highest level. We want to innovate and improve medicine and specifically neurosurgery at the very highest level. And that's what's going to make the difference here is we're going to be highly focused. Thank you so much Dr. Yosher. Absolutely a fascinating segment and thank you so much for joining us today. After a few months of (indistinct) work, I was panicked. I had left medicine and I was not exactly changing the world. I felt like an outsider. I was ready to throw in the towel and return to school. On one dark rainy night, I called Shivam and told her I'd made a big mistake and wanted to return to Penn where I felt comfortable and valued. She talked me out of leaving, and over the next few months, I kept at it. I eventually got a proper job on the campaign and for a few hours late in the evening on election night, I even thought I was headed to The White House to work for a president. Of course, it didn't work out that way. By January I was back in West Philadelphia. But my worldview had changed. And so had my life plan. I was better able to understand that as unsettling and risky as change can feel, I needed that experience to pursue my real calling. Instead of doing a residency, I was asked by someone I met on the campaign to join a new foundation created by Bill and Melinda Gates. There, I got to be part of the team that set an audacious goal. That every child, everywhere should be fully vaccinated. To do so we built new partnerships across industry, governments and NGOs and we invented new ways to finance and procure vaccines. These efforts saved millions of lives and created a template for the development and distribution of COVID-19 vaccines today. A few years later, I joined the Obama administration. As a newcomer to Washington, that unsettling feeling of uncertainty, occasionally returned. When I was was overseeing America's response to the earthquake in Haiti, negotiating aid arrangements alongside the military in Afghanistan, and searching for new solutions to break transmission rates early in the Ebola pandemic. Each of these tasks involved embracing change. Trying new ways to solve problems and asking others to embrace risk and uncertainty. On reflection, I really believe my most satisfying and successful professional experiences have all been grounded in setting big goals, taking risks and above of all, embracing change. I hope you will have those opportunities in your endeavors. The second story I wanna tell you is about using your voice. A few months after I started at the Rockefeller Foundation in March of 2017, I was in New Orleans where I met mayor Mitch Landrieu. We talked about how New Orleans, like many cities around America, was not only plagued by systemic racism and violence, but also stained by monuments to the Confederacy. Mayor Landrieu asked that the Rockefeller Foundation provided a grant to help take down four Confederate monuments including a towering statue of Robert E. Lee. I was less than 10 weeks into my job at one of the most storied foundations in America. And I was excited at the opportunity to make a mark on such an important issue. But when I started making calls that night to discuss removing the statues, all I heard was how doing so was complicated. It was complicated because, as one philanthropic leader argued, many of those with the deepest pockets in New Orleans like the statues just fine and might not support our future partnerships. It was complicated because of some on our team worried white supremacists might take aim at Rockefeller Foundation offices and we didn't have the security to protect our staff. And it was complicated because the foundation hadn't worked on racial justice issues in recent years and we were worried about looking naive on such a complex public issue. Making a statement is often complicated. for a time growing up, my family lived in rural Pennsylvania. I was the one Brown kid on a big yellow school bus filled with white children. On most days I got on that bus sat in the back and felt like I didn't belong. I stayed quiet. You see if I didn't attract attention, I would be like it's likely to be called names, made fun of or worse. I hated that feeling. Anyone who knows me know staying quiet comes at great difficulty. So when I woke up in New Orleans the next morning, I went for a short jog to see the statue of Lee which had stood cross armed and defiance since 1884. As I stood there in the shadows of both the Confederacy and my own experience, I decided that I wanted to do what I could to ensure children in New Orleans no longer had to walk to school under the watchful eye of a Confederate general. I wanted to use the new found authority in my role to make a statement. So Rockefeller made the grant and one month later to the day the statues came down. From that day forward, our country engaged in a debate about monuments and statues, and other communities followed New Orleans lead. Unfortunately not long after, a counter reaction began as white nationalists rallied with torches in Charlottesville, Virginia to save another Lee statue. And later the proud boys marched across the country including in Philadelphia, clearly helping to take down a few offensive monuments did not end racism in America but it was the right thing to do. After today's ceremony, other people will address each of you as doctor for the rest of your lives. Congratulations, you've earned it. In this country and around the world, that title immediately confers respect and authority. It is the authority that comes with knowing how to heal a suffering patient at their greatest moment of need. But it's also a signal that you're a leader, in your community, in your institutions, in our country and in our world. Your voice matters. I hope you will use it to do the right thing. When I look back on that long drive to Nashville and that short jog in New Orleans, I'm reminded of how much we all must change ourselves in order to realize the change we want to see in the world. I hope you keep taking risks, keep learning, keep growing and keep changing. As you do, there will be moments of panic, moments when you'll wonder what you've gotten yourself into. My advice to you, is to go find those moments, when you're at the edge of who you are, and what you can do for your patients, your community and our common humanity. And when you get there, keep going, embrace that change because I found we all need to re-imagine who we are and what we want this world to be, perhaps now more than ever. I and all of my classmates in the class of 1971 the 50th reunion class extend our sincere congratulations to each of you in the 2021 graduating class. Having been in your shoes 50 years ago, the class of 1971 is proud of what you have accomplished and is excited for you as you move beyond medical school and enter training for medical careers in the 21st century. A famous baseball player once said, quote, "It is tough to make predictions especially about the future." How true it is as I reflect over the 50 years since I graduated medical school. Most of our class entered medical school right after college primarily as science majors. I was one of only 12 women in a class of 126 students. We graduated after four years and had a small number of MD, PhDs and no joint master degree certificate programs or significant global experiences were offered or available during medical school. In medical school, we were taught primarily with in-person lectures from professors otherwise known as the sage on the stage, taking notes as fast as we could, learning from textbooks which we all bought. One so heavy we could not carry them to school and memorizing lots of information, never sure what was important or when we would need to recall specific facts. Our lectures and labs took place in the basement of the John Morgan building on Hamilton walk. We could not have predicted your experience 50 years later which was quite different from ours. Your class was not only more diverse than ours, but had 48% women, 60% or more of you were non-traditional students having taken time off before entering medical school, teaching and learning, utilize technology, which made lectures and textbooks virtual and available on your iphones, iPads and laptop computers 24/7 during medical school. And 2/3 of your class participated in joint programs leading to an MD plus degree, MD, PhDs, master's degrees, certificates and or global health experiences. Your educational space was now the Jordan Medical Education Center. An innovative learning and teaching environment with state-of-the-art technology for collaborative, team-based active learning. Comparing your experience in medical school with ours clearly shows that medical education has been changed forever and most likely will continue to change. Our experience in the healthcare environment since we graduated, portends, transformative and revolutionary change that I believe will now impact your experience in health care. What will healthcare change mean for you, the class of 2021? No surprise, with medical information expanding exponentially and available almost immediately because of technology, the skill needed to succeed in medicine is being a self-directed learner. In 2010 medical knowledge doubled every 3 and 1/2 years. And in 2020 medical knowledge doubled every 73 days. That was last year. Therefore, almost all that we learned and much of what you learned recently in medical school, maybe obsolete shortly. You are prepared for accessing expanding medical knowledge because of the school of medicines learning for life curriculum, which emphasized active and self-directed learning utilizing technology. Such continued lifelong learning will be necessary to stay up to date on whatever new knowledge is generated. Learning experiences for medical students, trainees and faculty will continue to move away from real time in-person experiences with patients and be replaced with virtual experiences, simulations, augmented reality and telemedicine. The concept from my class of quote, "see one, do one ,teach one." Unquote, is no longer viable. Your class will need to be involved in continuous practice and training throughout your careers to learn new techniques and procedures. To help you keep up and be at the top of your game. Virtual training experiences will play an important role in your future. Add to all of these changes the delivery of healthcare is changing so rapidly that it is impossible to know how medical care will be delivered in 10 years, nevermind 50 years. We learned and practiced primarily acute care medicine in the hospital setting. But already for you healthcare has moved beyond the hospital to outpatient facilities, surgery centers and even into patient's homes. Wearable devices that can transmit patient information directly to a doctor's office, blood pressure heart rate EKGs are becoming a commonplace. The importance and recognition of social determinants of disease and environmental factors in causing disease will result in new early treatment modalities. More importantly, patients will be taken care of by teams of healthcare providers instead of just a single physician, which will change forever, the doctor-patient relationship. Most of us trained to become clinicians in either private practice or academic medicine, but with the changes occurring in the healthcare during the last 20 years, many of us took on different roles and became part of the change process. My first appointment at Penn medicine was as a nephrologist involved in patient care teaching and clinical research. With my strong interest in medical education and teaching I was selected in 1995 to be the inaugural vice Dean for Education for the Perelman School of Medicine. In that role, I oversaw the design and implementation of the present educational model, learning for life, initially called curriculum 2000, virtual curriculum 2000 and the design of the Jordan Medical Education Center. I could not have predicted that career path for me when I graduated medical school, since that path did not even exist, but I cannot imagine having had a more exciting and creative career. I encourage all of you to be on the lookout for changing medical career opportunities that will excite you, allow you to use your creative talents and let you all make an impact in and on the world of medicine. Last but not least maintaining your mental and physical health is crucial to your success. Doctors in general tend to take care of everyone except themselves. They take care of patients, family, friends, staff and all others. We never learned about wellness for ourselves or the importance of work-life balance. I don't remember ever having a lecture on sleep, probably irrelevant since it's insurance we were on every other night. But you all know better. You know, you need to take care of yourself and it is important that each of you determine how you can best achieve that in a world of healthcare that is constantly changing. So it was Yogi Berra, not a physician you said, it is tough to make predictions especially about the future. I don't know in 2071 who will be your 50th year speaker, nor what specific changes will be in place for medical education and healthcare, but there will be transformative and revolutionary changes to both. Your class is unique and what you have experienced the last year of medical school because of the COVID 19 pandemic, that all of you have adapted to disruptive changes in the delivery of healthcare while in medical school and still accomplished and completed all that you did is remarkable. And as a statement to you being prepared for the continued change to the medical world, you will enter. I do know today May 16th, 2021, is a time not to now to think about the future, but to celebrate today and all of your accomplishments and successes. My congratulations to all of you and a special thank you to your family, significant others and friends who have supported you along the way. From the trustees of the university of Pennsylvania to Deans Jameson and Rose, and the dedicated members of the undergraduate medical education leadership team and the program for diversity and inclusion, not to mention the many faculty residents and fellows who have supported us on our journeys. To the family and friends here to support us today, welcome, more importantly, thank you. We would never have made it through to this day that we have all been waiting for. Your patients through the sleepless nights, endless study dates, specialty choice woes, and match day anxieties got us through. Know that for every graduate receiving their degree today you are the people who deserve their own diplomas. Finally, to my class, I can't believe it, we're here. Opening my regalia I was so overcome with emotion that I honestly couldn't even try it on. Finally, the tears came, tears of joy and relief. After so many years where here, I am so proud of you. I'm proud of us. We survived the 04:00 a.m. wake ups, the exams, the adventure of Zoom residency interviews. We did it all. I don't know that any of us will ever look at a space bar the same way again, but we made it. We have been through so much this past year. Most of it unexpected. For me, that includes the unexpected death of my father last Summer. Confronting death is among the hardest things we deal with in medicine and as human beings. The last year year has brought more loss upon our communities than I thought possible and I know I'm not the only one trying to make sense of what has happened. As students, as a country, as a world we have been through so much. That said just as we learned from the death of every patient, so to have I learned from the death of my father, as painful as it was. My dad was my first teacher in medicine. He was a surgeon at a small community hospital where he'd been working for 15 years. And when I think of what I hope to embody in medicine, I think of him. I hope to share some of that wisdom with you in the form of the lessons that my father taught me about medicine. The first lesson is that, while what we do is serious, it also has its joys if we're open to seeing them. Medicine is full of moments of connection, intimacy, and even laughter. As one of my favorite residents was fond of saying to me, humor is a mature defense. Sometimes all we can do is laugh. There was a time when grateful for his services, one of my father's patients dropped off two live chickens at our house as a token of appreciation. Needless to say our neighbors were not thrilled with this but my father shrugged it off with a laugh. When faced with the absurd and unbelievable he always chuckled. Ever unflappable, there really wasn't much that could get under his skin. And with that in mind, on the numerous occasions where I literally followed my resident to the bathroom or the mortifying moment, when I standing with a newborn baby in one hand and an (indistinct) scope in the other suddenly realized I didn't know what to do with either of them. I laughed. I learned from my father that life is too short to take it too seriously. And I've learned from my patients that sometimes all we need is laughter to lighten the mood and the day. So when you spend half an hour fretting over your first momentous order of Tylenol or laxatives, smile at yourself and remember that your seniors always have your back. The second lesson is that, there's a reason that we, brand new to our short white coats and medicine spent these last four years or more for my MD, PhD friends, working together in teams. That's because at the end of the day medicine is a team sport. This is true now more than ever. COVID has taught us that each one of us from the environmental services workers to the nurses the respiratory therapists, to the cafeteria staff is essential to the functioning of our healthcare system. It doesn't work unless we're all here and it especially doesn't work if we're not in it together. My dad's funeral was attended by everyone from the environmental services staff to the OR techs to the CEO of the hospital. He befriended everyone, and he understood that working in healthcare means working well with all members of the care team. Medicine is already wildly different from when I first put on my short white coat 10 years ago, but one thing is true, we will be more successful working together than we will be divided. As an intern remember that everyone is part of the team, and if we do it right, we do together. Never forget when you've completely forgotten which line is which, that a long time nurse is your best friend. And also it never hurts to make friends with the people who know where the coffee is. Finally remember that we are all part of something larger. And this year, while unprecedented has merely revealed lessons that we should carry with us for the rest of our careers. For medical students, this moment has shown us that the best laid plans are always subject to change, yet amidst the turmoil of career paths have ended and transformed, we should remember that the core maxims of our profession, to aid our fellow human and do no harm, remain. We may be living through unsteady, uncertain times but remaining grounded in our principles helps us to focus on what matters. Penn medicine has taught us above all to be leaders in medicine. And so as we move on to this next stage in our training, what do you want to hold dear? What matters to you about being a physician? In these next few months, the calm before the storm we have a unique opportunity to solidify our values and pledge to commit to them. As the future of medicine, we can help shape our field for years to come. We are an integral part of rebuilding a world that is more equitable and just. This feels daunting, but in moments of uncertainty I always returned to the Jewish proverb. "You are not obligated to complete the work but neither are you free to abandon it." We all have a role. The challenge is finding it. Congratulations, everyone. We made it. - Thank you, Dr. Munyikwa. for your powerful words and your inspiring message. Across the globe, people are missing spending time with their family and friends, sending their children to school. Many are missing a job, a paycheck. And most importantly, more and more are missing a loved one who has been lost to COVID-19. But even as we recognize and honor those losses today, I have no doubt that this medical school graduation, the graduation of 2020, will be remembered first and foremost not for what we have lost, but for what we have been given-- the chance to begin and to begin again. For your class, it is the chance to begin your career at a time of national crisis when your humanity and your skills have never been more needed. For medicine, it is the chance to begin again as a field, to begin a new era for medicine, to define what medicine can do for our patients, our communities, and our society. What it means to be a doctor today. Even though it has been almost 30 years since I stood in your shoes, I have strong memories of medical school. Some of those memories are concrete, even visceral-- memories of rooms, and people, and smells. But my strongest memories are of feelings-- the combination of fear, excitement, and humility when I first walked into a room to take a history from a sick patient, the growing anticipation that I am sure you all are feeling now of when I would be the doctor, not a student doctor anymore. But my deepest feelings was a growing sense of awe-- awe about what it means to join a profession that is dedicated to serving others-- as you will say in the oath later today, to dedicate our lives to the service of humanity. Medical school was also when I began to understand that this profession, united in its goal of serving humanity, often approached that goal from two parallel worlds. Of course, I now know that this medical dualism has been recognized for centuries and the descriptions, of course, have varied across time and setting. Sometimes, it's called the art and science of medicine. Sometimes, the worlds of mind and body. Sometimes, the power of data and the power of stories. Increasingly, the biological and social determinants of health. In the end, all of these words are seeking to describe a fundamental truth-- the truth that both disease and circumstance matter, or to paraphrase William Osler, we must both know what sort of patient has a disease and what sort of a disease a patient has. We know here today, as you stand graduating and becoming a doctor, that the health of our patients is driven both by the behavior of molecules and by the behavior of humans, driven both by biology and by society. Nothing, of course, could have brought that truth home more clearly than the experience of the last months. While the SARS-CoV-2 infection would not exist without the COVID-19 virus, there is no doubt that the impact of that virus on our patients and our communities has been driven by social forces, particularly the long-standing structural inequities across racial and ethnic groups in the US. In Boston, our hardest-hit community Chelsea became a hotspot not because of a change in virus biology, but because it is impossible to self-quarantine when you have no food and eight people live in a one-room apartment. One of the greatest accomplishments of the last 70 years has been our ability-- the medical profession's ability-- to change fundamental human biology. We now target proteins to change their function, turn on and off the immune system, reprogram cells to create miniature organs, remove parts of the body that are causing disease, and replace them sometimes with man-made new parts. We have harnessed scientific advances to prevent illness, cure disease, and relieve suffering far beyond anything that I could have imagined when I stood in your shoes almost 30 years ago. Unfortunately, the same story cannot be told for the other world in which we live. In fact, paradoxically, over the last decades, we have become a profession that believes that we can transform fundamental human biology, but are relatively helpless against social forces, incapable of changing the man-made social structures that drive health, a profession that believes we can edit specific genes and specific tissues to prevent heart disease, but cannot provide high-quality health care for all, that we can redirect immune responses to cure metastatic cancer, but cannot ensure that our patients can afford their medications, that we can grow an organ in a dish, but cannot address racism in health care, that we can replace heart valves or even an entire aorta when needed, but cannot not provide mental health care to those in need. Honestly, this has never made sense to me. How can we feel so empowered to take on fundamental biology, but so disempowered when faced with the human and social processes that we ourselves created? At least those were the two worlds that we lived in until the last several months, until the COVID-19 pandemic, until the year of your medical school graduation because we have seen over the last months that, in fact, we can take on these processes. In the matter of weeks, we have transformed the health care system. We created hospitals in parking lots and shut down practices that we did not need. We turned orthopedic surgeons, and internists, and primary care nurses into critical care experts. We brought medical care to patients wherever they needed it, using whatever modality that we needed. We train new skills overnight using Zoom and some well-curated handouts. But perhaps most importantly, we came together. We came together across disciplines, across countries, and across institutions that have competed for generations. We did it because it was right, it was needed, and it was what a doctor should do. Although there are many stories of courage and commitment that will be told about the pandemic, none are more inspiring to me than how medical students have risen to this challenge. You and your colleagues have volunteered to track patients across settings, to staff hotlines and pagers, to develop new tools to support health care workers, to provide support for vulnerable populations, including food and quarantine supplies. These stories are important to me not only because what you have contributed to the COVID-19 epidemic, but because of what it says about you, the Graduating Class of 2020. It says that you understand that we can do much more than we thought. Yes, we can edit genes. Yes, we can target proteins. Yes, we can turn on and off the immune system. But you also know that we can get patients the care that they need. We can work across a city to take care of our most vulnerable populations. We can stand up housing for those who have nowhere else to recover. Yes, we can do what is needed and what is right. As inspired as I am about what has been accomplished over the last months, I know that this is just a beginning and that the path ahead will not be easy. There have been many, many years of believing that such changes were out of our reach. There are deep structural issues and perverse incentives. The complexity of health care-- comprehensive health care for all-- is far greater than even the most complicated response to COVID-19. We have our work cut out for us. Today, you graduate from the nation's first medical school. For well over 250 years, the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine, now called the Perelman has led this country in defining medical education, defining what it means to be a doctor. You should be incredibly proud. It is now your turn to take up this mantle, to build upon what you have learned over the last years and what you have seen and accomplished over the last months to lead our country in service to our patients, our communities, and yes, to humanity, using and creating every tool that is needed because after all, that is what a doctor does. You will have up days and down days in medicine. One day, you'll save a patient's life by diagnosing a brain tumor from simple clinical findings in the office.
